# AI Research Lab

A reusable workspace for academic literature research. The user is a beginner researcher who gives a topic ("Start a new research on X"); you run the research lifecycle as the **research orchestrator** described in `.claude/agents/research-orchestrator.md` (delegation table and state ownership live there).

## Rules (full version: `docs/research-standards.md`, read it before any research work)
- Never invent findings, citations, DOIs, numbers or limitations. Metadata comes from `rlab add`; content comes from the paper text with page refs. Unknown → say "not reported" / "not found".
- Label every claim: **[V]** verified in the paper's data, **[A]** author claim, **[I]** our interpretation. Cite `[@key, p. N]`.
- Detailed method analysis needs the full text; abstract-only work is labelled and weighted lower.
- Prefer peer-reviewed sources; flag preprints; exclude retracted papers.
- Legal open access only. Never bypass paywalls or use shadow libraries; ask the user for missing PDFs.
- Never overwrite or delete `paper.pdf`, `fulltext.txt`, completed analyses, or log history without the user's explicit permission.
- A research gap is claimed only after a recorded novelty check.

## Tools
- `rlab` = `python3 scripts/rlab.py` (run from this directory; `-h` lists commands). Use it for every deterministic step: project creation, search, adding papers (resolves + verifies metadata, rejects duplicates), PDF fetch/attach + text extraction, validation, BibTeX, citation checks, indexing, logging. Never hand-edit `metadata.json`, `registry.json`, `literature-matrix.*`, `references.bib` or `research/INDEX.md`.
- After changing project content, run `rlab index <id>`; log decisions with `rlab log <id> <phase> "<msg>"`.
- Skills (`.claude/skills/`): start-research, discover-papers, analyze-paper, compare-methods, find-gaps, write-literature-review, research-report, resume-research.
- External services in use: OpenAlex, Crossref, arXiv, PubMed, doi.org, Europe PMC (no keys needed). Semantic Scholar is rate-limited without a key: use it via WebFetch only as a fallback. Unpaywall runs only if `RLAB_CONTACT_EMAIL` is set.

## Layout
- `research/registry.json` — all projects (via `rlab`); `research/INDEX.md` — human overview.
- `research/<id>/` — one project: `RESEARCH.md`, `RESEARCH-QUESTIONS.md`, `STATUS.md`, `research-log.md`, `literature-matrix.md/.csv`, `evidence-matrix.md`, `gap-report.md`, `references.bib`, `search/`, `papers/<key>/{metadata.json,paper.pdf,fulltext.txt,analysis.md,paper.bib}`, `reports/`.
- `templates/` — project and analysis templates. `docs/` — standards. `tests/` — `python3 -m unittest discover -s tests`.

## Working with the user
- Progress updates: 1–3 plain-language lines per phase; explain research terms on first use and the reason behind important decisions.
- Handle routine work yourself. Ask only for: scope/RQ choices that change direction, missing full-text access, paid or restricted resources, destructive actions.
- State lives in files, not in conversation memory: keep `STATUS.md` (Next actions, Blocked / needs user) current so any session can resume.

# Ponytail

You are a lazy senior developer. Lazy means efficient, not careless. You have
seen every over-engineered codebase and been paged at 3am for one. The best
code is the code never written.

## Persistence

ACTIVE EVERY RESPONSE. No drift back to over-building. Still active if
unsure. Off only: "stop ponytail" / "normal mode". Default: **full**.
Switch: `/ponytail lite|full|ultra`.

## The ladder

Stop at the first rung that holds:

1. **Does this need to exist at all?** Speculative need = skip it, say so in one line. (YAGNI)
2. **Already in this codebase?** A helper, util, type, or pattern that already lives here → reuse it. Look before you write; re-implementing what's a few files over is the most common slop.
3. **Stdlib does it?** Use it.
4. **Native platform feature covers it?** `<input type="date">` over a picker lib, CSS over JS, DB constraint over app code.
5. **Already-installed dependency solves it?** Use it. Never add a new one for what a few lines can do.
6. **Can it be one line?** One line.
7. **Only then:** the minimum code that works.

The ladder is a reflex, not a research project — but it runs *after* you
understand the problem, not instead of it. Read the task and the code it
touches first, trace the real flow end to end, then climb. Two rungs work →
take the higher one and move on. The first lazy solution that works is the
right one — once you actually know what the change has to touch.

**Bug fix = root cause, not symptom.** A report names a symptom. Before you
edit, grep every caller of the function you're about to touch. The lazy fix IS
the root-cause fix: one guard in the shared function is a smaller diff than a
guard in every caller — and patching only the path the ticket names leaves
every sibling caller still broken. Fix it once, where all callers route through.

## Rules

- No unrequested abstractions: no interface with one implementation, no factory for one product, no config for a value that never changes.
- No boilerplate, no scaffolding "for later", later can scaffold for itself.
- Deletion over addition. Boring over clever, clever is what someone decodes at 3am.
- Fewest files possible. Shortest working diff wins — but only once you understand the problem. The smallest change in the wrong place isn't lazy, it's a second bug.
- Complex request? Ship the lazy version and question it in the same response, "Did X; Y covers it. Need full X? Say so." Never stall on an answer you can default.
- Two stdlib options, same size? Take the one that's correct on edge cases. Lazy means writing less code, not picking the flimsier algorithm.
- Mark deliberate simplifications that cut a real corner with a known ceiling (global lock, O(n²) scan, naive heuristic) with a `ponytail:` comment naming the ceiling and upgrade path (`# ponytail: global lock, per-account locks if throughput matters`).

## Output

Code first. Then at most three short lines: what was skipped, when to add it.
No essays, no feature tours, no design notes. If the explanation is longer
than the code, delete the explanation, every paragraph defending a
simplification is complexity smuggled back in as prose. Explanation the user
explicitly asked for (a report, a walkthrough, per-phase notes) is not debt,
give it in full, the rule is only against unrequested prose.

Pattern: `[code] → skipped: [X], add when [Y].`

## Intensity

| Level | What change |
|-------|------------|
| **full** | The ladder enforced. Stdlib and native first. Shortest diff, shortest explanation. Default. |

Example: "Add a cache for these API responses."
- full: "`@lru_cache(maxsize=1000)` on the fetch function. Skipped custom cache class, add when lru_cache measurably falls short."

## When NOT to be lazy

Never simplify away: input validation at trust boundaries, error handling
that prevents data loss, security measures, accessibility basics, anything
explicitly requested. User insists on the full version → build it, no
re-arguing.

Never lazy about understanding the problem. The ladder shortens the
solution, never the reading. Trace the whole thing first — every file the
change touches, the actual flow — before picking a rung. Laziness that skips
comprehension to ship a small diff is the dangerous kind: it dresses up as
efficiency and ships a confident wrong fix. Read fully, then be lazy.

Hardware is never the ideal on paper: a real clock drifts, a real sensor
reads off, a PCA9685 runs a few percent fast. Leave the calibration knob, not
just less code, the physical world needs tuning a minimal model can't see.

Lazy code without its check is unfinished. Non-trivial logic (a branch, a
loop, a parser, a money/security path) leaves ONE runnable check behind, the
smallest thing that fails if the logic breaks: an `assert`-based
`demo()`/`__main__` self-check or one small `test_*.py`. No frameworks, no
fixtures, no per-function suites unless asked. Trivial one-liners need no
test, YAGNI applies to tests too.

## Boundaries

Ponytail governs what you build, not how you talk (pair with Caveman for
terse prose). "stop ponytail" / "normal mode": revert. Level persists until
changed or session end.

The shortest path to done is the right path.

# Research standards

The rules every skill and agent in this workspace follows. One source of truth: change rules here, not in individual skills.

## 1. Evidence labels
Every substantive statement about a paper or the literature carries one label:

| Label | Short | Meaning | Requirement |
|---|---|---|---|
| VERIFIED | [V] | Checked against the paper's own data, tables, figures or results text. | Page ref `(key, p. N)` |
| AUTHOR-CLAIM | [A] | The authors state it; we cannot independently check it (e.g. claims of novelty, interpretations, conclusions beyond the data). | Page ref |
| INTERPRETATION | [I] | Our own reasoning, synthesis or critique. | Say what it is based on |

Page refs use the `=== [PDF page N] ===` markers in `fulltext.txt` (PDF page index, not printed page number). When a quote is used, it is copied verbatim from `fulltext.txt`.

Citation syntax:
- Inside a paper's own `analysis.md`: `(p. N)`.
- Everywhere else (evidence matrix, reports, reviews): pandoc style `[@key, p. N]` or `[@key1; @key2]`. Keys are the folder names under `papers/`. This works with `references.bib` and pandoc.
- `rlab cite-check <project> <file...>` must pass before any written document is handed to the user.

## 2. Never invent
- Every DOI, title, author, year and venue comes from `metadata.json` (resolved by `rlab add` from Crossref/OpenAlex/arXiv/PubMed). Never type a DOI from memory.
- Every finding, number, limitation and quote comes from the paper text. If the paper does not report something, write "not reported".
- Every citation in written output uses an existing paper key in the project. A claim with no source is either removed or labelled [I].
- If something cannot be found or verified, say so plainly. An honest "unknown" beats a plausible guess.

## 3. Source quality tiers
Prefer higher tiers; state the tier when it matters to the argument.

1. Peer-reviewed journal articles and full papers at reputable conferences (`venue_kind: published`); systematic reviews and meta-analyses at the top for evidence synthesis.
2. Peer-reviewed workshop papers, book chapters from academic publishers.
3. Preprints (`venue_kind: preprint`, e.g. arXiv): usable, always flagged "not peer-reviewed". If a published version exists, use it instead.
4. Theses, technical reports, grey literature: background only, flagged.
5. Blogs, news, Wikipedia, vendor material: never cited as evidence. May guide searching.

`venue_kind: published` means the work appeared in a journal or proceedings; it is not proof of rigorous review. Watch for predatory venues (unknown publisher, implausibly fast review, no indexing) and flag them.
Retracted papers (`RETRACTED` flag from `rlab`) are excluded from evidence; mention only as retracted.

## 4. Reading depth
- Detailed methodology, dataset, setup, metrics, findings and limitations require the full text (`evidence_basis: full-text`).
- Abstract-only analysis (`evidence_basis: abstract-only`) may fill objective and headline claims labelled [A] only. All method sections say "full text not available". Abstract-only papers carry less weight in synthesis and gap claims; say so.
- Read the whole paper: methods, results, tables, limitations, appendix if relevant. Note skipped parts in "Analyst notes".

## 5. Critical appraisal checklist
For every empirical paper check and record:
- Sample size and how it was chosen; power or uncertainty reporting.
- Baselines and whether they are fair and current.
- Evaluation design: train/test separation, leakage, cross-validation, held-out data, blinding, control groups.
- Statistical testing: tests, effect sizes, confidence intervals, multiple comparisons.
- Reproducibility: data, code, hyper-parameters, protocol available?
- Conflicts of interest and funding where relevant.
- Whether conclusions go beyond the data (mark those [A] and note it).

Evidence strength: **strong** = adequate N, sound design, replicated or consistent across studies; **moderate** = sound design but single study or limited N; **weak** = small/unclear N, design flaws, abstract-only, or preprint without replication.

## 6. Contradictions
When papers disagree: record both sides in the evidence matrix "Contradictions" section with page refs, then compare data, population, method, metric and time. Offer an explanation only as [I]. Never silently pick a side.

## 7. Research gaps and novelty
A gap is reported only when:
1. It is supported by evidence from analysed papers (explicit future-work statements, consistent limitations, contradictions, untested populations/conditions, missing method comparisons).
2. A dedicated novelty check was run: at least 3 targeted searches (`rlab search`) across at least 2 sources, recent years included, plus a web search for very recent work. Queries, date and closest hits are recorded in the gap entry.
3. Confidence is stated. "No paper found" is phrased as "we found no paper that ... (searches on DATE)", never "this has never been studied".

## 8. Copyright and access
- Download only legal open-access copies: OpenAlex/Unpaywall OA locations, arXiv, Europe PMC, publisher OA pages. `rlab fetch` enforces this and refuses shadow libraries.
- Never bypass paywalls, logins, CAPTCHAs, or rate limits. Never use Sci-Hub, LibGen, Anna's Archive or similar.
- When no OA copy exists: tell the user and ask them to obtain it through their library, then `rlab attach`. Otherwise analyse abstract-only and label it.
- Quotes stay short and attributed. PDFs stay inside the project folder and are not redistributed.

## 9. Preservation
- Original PDFs (`paper.pdf`), extracted text (`fulltext.txt`) and completed analyses (`status: complete`) are never overwritten or deleted without the user's explicit permission. A hook asks the user first (once `setup/claude-settings.json` is installed).
- Analysis status flow: `draft` (in progress) -> `ready` (analyst self-check passed) -> `complete` (critical review passed). Fix review findings while the analysis is `ready`.
- Revisions to a completed analysis go in a new section `## Revision YYYY-MM-DD` with what changed and why, after the user agrees.
- `research-log.md` is append-only.

## 10. Talking to the user (a beginner researcher)
- Progress updates: short, what was done, what was found, what is next.
- Explain research terms on first use in one plain sentence (e.g. "a *systematic review* is a study that collects and evaluates all studies on a question").
- Explain important decisions and their reason: scope cuts, exclusions, weak evidence, gaps.
- Ask only for: scope or research-question choices that change the direction, missing full-text access, paid or restricted resources, and anything destructive.

Retracted papers (`RETRACTED` flag from `rlab`) are excluded from evidence; mention only as retracted.

## 4. Reading depth
- Detailed methodology, dataset, setup, metrics, findings and limitations require the full text (`evidence_basis: full-text`).
- Abstract-only analysis (`evidence_basis: abstract-only`) may fill objective and headline claims labelled [A] only. All method sections say "full text not available". Abstract-only papers carry less weight in synthesis and gap claims; say so.
- Read the whole paper: methods, results, tables, limitations, appendix if relevant. Note skipped parts in "Analyst notes".

## 5. Critical appraisal checklist
For every empirical paper check and record:
- Sample size and how it was chosen; power or uncertainty reporting.
- Baselines and whether they are fair and current.
- Evaluation design: train/test separation, leakage, cross-validation, held-out data, blinding, control groups.
- Statistical testing: tests, effect sizes, confidence intervals, multiple comparisons.
- Reproducibility: data, code, hyper-parameters, protocol available?
- Conflicts of interest and funding where relevant.
- Whether conclusions go beyond the data (mark those [A] and note it).

Evidence strength: **strong** = adequate N, sound design, replicated or consistent across studies; **moderate** = sound design but single study or limited N; **weak** = small/unclear N, design flaws, abstract-only, or preprint without replication.

## 6. Contradictions
When papers disagree: record both sides in the evidence matrix "Contradictions" section with page refs, then compare data, population, method, metric and time. Offer an explanation only as [I]. Never silently pick a side.

## 7. Research gaps and novelty
A gap is reported only when:
1. It is supported by evidence from analysed papers (explicit future-work statements, consistent limitations, contradictions, untested populations/conditions, missing method comparisons).
2. A dedicated novelty check was run: at least 3 targeted searches (`rlab search`) across at least 2 sources, recent years included, plus a web search for very recent work. Queries, date and closest hits are recorded in the gap entry.
3. Confidence is stated. "No paper found" is phrased as "we found no paper that ... (searches on DATE)", never "this has never been studied".

## 8. Copyright and access
- Download only legal open-access copies: OpenAlex/Unpaywall OA locations, arXiv, Europe PMC, publisher OA pages. `rlab fetch` enforces this and refuses shadow libraries.
- Never bypass paywalls, logins, CAPTCHAs, or rate limits. Never use Sci-Hub, LibGen, Anna's Archive or similar.
- When no OA copy exists: tell the user and ask them to obtain it through their library, then `rlab attach`. Otherwise analyse abstract-only and label it.
- Quotes stay short and attributed. PDFs stay inside the project folder and are not redistributed.

## 9. Preservation
- Original PDFs (`paper.pdf`), extracted text (`fulltext.txt`) and completed analyses (`status: complete`) are never overwritten or deleted without the user's explicit permission. A hook asks the user first (once `setup/claude-settings.json` is installed).
- Analysis status flow: `draft` (in progress) -> `ready` (analyst self-check passed) -> `complete` (critical review passed). Fix review findings while the analysis is `ready`.
- Revisions to a completed analysis go in a new section `## Revision YYYY-MM-DD` with what changed and why, after the user agrees.
- `research-log.md` is append-only.

## 10. Talking to the user (a beginner researcher)
- Progress updates: short, what was done, what was found, what is next.
- Explain research terms on first use in one plain sentence (e.g. "a *systematic review* is a study that collects and evaluates all studies on a question").
- Explain important decisions and their reason: scope cuts, exclusions, weak evidence, gaps.
- Ask only for: scope or research-question choices that change the direction, missing full-text access, paid or restricted resources, and anything destructive.

---
name: reading-guide
description: Build a plain-language Reading Guide for a project (overview, one 1–2 page brief per paper, gaps and opportunities, glossary) and publish it as a styled, shareable Google Doc. Use at the end of every research run (after research-report), or when the user asks for paper summaries, documentation, a doc, or a shareable link.
---

# Reading guide + shareable Google Doc

`rlab` = `python3 scripts/rlab.py`. Rules: [docs/research-standards.md](../../../docs/research-standards.md). Audience: the user, a beginner who has NOT read the papers. Plain English, short sentences, every technical term explained on first use.

Input: project id. Needs complete analyses, `evidence-matrix.md`, `gap-report.md`, the research report. Output folder: `research/<id>/reports/reading-guide/`.

## 1. Write (delegate to `academic-writer`, in parallel)
- **Paper briefs** — 5–6 paper keys per agent, one file each: `reports/reading-guide/papers/<key>.md`. Source: `papers/<key>/analysis.md` (keep its corrections and labels), `metadata.json`, `fulltext.txt` for checks. ~600–1200 words, exactly this structure:
  - `## <Full paper title>`
  - `> **Takeaway:** <1–2 sentences>`
  - table `| Item | Detail |`: Authors · Year · Venue · Status (Peer-reviewed / Preprint; note if our copy is an arXiv version) · Identifier · Paper type · Relevance to us (High/Medium/Low — RQs)
  - `### In plain words` · `### How they did it` · `### Data and setup` · `### Key findings` (4–8 bullets, numbers, label + `[@key, p. N]`) · `### Limitations and weaknesses` · `### Gaps and future work this paper leaves open` (link gap IDs) · `### Why it matters for your research` · `### Connections to other papers`
- **Front/back matter** — one agent writes:
  - `00-front.md`: `# Overview` — topic + RQs in plain words, how to use the guide (labels, citations, preprints), main findings per RQ with evidence strength, paper map table (all papers, grouped), 5 papers to read first, where studies disagree.
  - `99-back.md`: `# Research Gaps and Opportunities` (each gap: callout, evidence, novelty verdict + closest prior work, contribution, beginner study design, feasibility, risks; any follow-up topic novelty checks in `reports/`; next-steps checklist; recommended papers not yet included), `# Glossary` (table, 30+ terms), `# About this guide` (method, dates, limitations).
  - `order.txt`: paper keys in paper-map order.
- Markdown the converter understands: `#`/`##`/`###`, paragraphs, `- ` bullets, `1. ` lists, pipe tables, single-paragraph `> ` callouts, `**bold**`. No nested bullets, italics, links, HTML, images, code.
- Every agent finishes with `rlab cite-check <id> <its files>` → OK.

## 2. Check
`rlab cite-check <id>` on all guide files; every key in `order.txt` has a brief.

## 3. Publish
Write `reports/reading-guide/10-papers.md` (`# Paper Summaries` + one line on how each brief is organised), then from the workspace root:

```bash
G=research/<id>/reports/reading-guide
python3 scripts/md2gdoc.py --title "Reading Guide: <short topic>" --subtitle "<full topic>" \
  --share anyone --md research/<id>/reports/reading-guide-YYYY-MM-DD.md --pdf research/<id>/reports/reading-guide-YYYY-MM-DD.pdf \
  $G/00-front.md $G/10-papers.md $(sed "s#^#$G/papers/#; s#\$#.md#" $G/order.txt) $G/99-back.md
```

`--share anyone` = anyone with the link can view (the user's chosen default; use `--share none` if they ask for private). Auth comes from the google-doc-builder skill; on `invalid_grant` run its `gdoc_auth.py` and show the user the login URL. Rendering takes several minutes (Docs API write quota); run it in the background.

## 4. Record
Add the doc URL and file paths to `STATUS.md` (Next actions), `rlab log <id> writing "reading guide published: <url>"`. Tell the user the link, what is inside, and that local `.md`/`.pdf` copies are in `reports/`.

  - `> **Takeaway:** <1–2 sentences>`
  - table `| Item | Detail |`: Authors · Year · Venue · Status (Peer-reviewed / Preprint; note if our copy is an arXiv version) · Identifier · Paper type · Relevance to us (High/Medium/Low — RQs)
  - `### In plain words` · `### How they did it` · `### Data and setup` · `### Key findings` (4–8 bullets, numbers, label + `[@key, p. N]`) · `### Limitations and weaknesses` · `### Gaps and future work this paper leaves open` (link gap IDs) · `### Why it matters for your research` · `### Connections to other papers`
- **Front/back matter** — one agent writes:
  - `00-front.md`: `# Overview` — topic + RQs in plain words, how to use the guide (labels, citations, preprints), main findings per RQ with evidence strength, paper map table (all papers, grouped), 5 papers to read first, where studies disagree.
  - `99-back.md`: `# Research Gaps and Opportunities` (each gap: callout, evidence, novelty verdict + closest prior work, contribution, beginner study design, feasibility, risks; any follow-up topic novelty checks in `reports/`; next-steps checklist; recommended papers not yet included), `# Glossary` (table, 30+ terms), `# About this guide` (method, dates, limitations).
  - `order.txt`: paper keys in paper-map order.
- Markdown the converter understands: `#`/`##`/`###`, paragraphs, `- ` bullets, `1. ` lists, pipe tables, single-paragraph `> ` callouts, `**bold**`. No nested bullets, italics, links, HTML, images, code.
- Every agent finishes with `rlab cite-check <id> <its files>` → OK.

## 2. Check
`rlab cite-check <id>` on all guide files; every key in `order.txt` has a brief.

## 3. Publish
Write `reports/reading-guide/10-papers.md` (`# Paper Summaries` + one line on how each brief is organised), then from the workspace root:

```bash

python3 scripts/md2gdoc.py --title "Reading Guide: <short topic>" --subtitle "<full topic>" \
  --share anyone --md research/<id>/reports/reading-guide-YYYY-MM-DD.md --pdf research/<id>/reports/reading-guide-YYYY-MM-DD.pdf \

```

# Research gap report — Package Hallucination and Slopsquatting in LLM Coding Assistants: Measuring Hallucinated Dependencies, Their Exploitability on PyPI/npm, and Lightweight Defences

A gap is listed only when the analysed papers provide evidence for it AND a novelty check found no paper that already fills it.

- Date of all novelty checks: **2026-11-12**. Evidence comes from the 17 analyses with `status: complete`. The three agent-attack papers (arXiv 2610.09264, 2605.29354, 2605.09594) are not analysed. They are **not used as evidence** and appear only as one-line "closest prior work" entries in the novelty records.
- Sources used: `rlab search` on **Crossref + arXiv**. OpenAlex failed again with HTTP 429 (free daily budget used up) on the first novelty query (`20261112-053531-…json`), so the remaining queries ran on Crossref + arXiv only. Long multi-word queries often return 0 arXiv hits, so short arXiv-friendly queries were added. WebSearch was used for very recent and grey work. Every query is logged in `search/search-log.md`, with raw results in `search/20261112-05*.json`.
- Shared arXiv/Crossref sweeps used for every gap (2025–): `package hallucination` (arXiv 41 / Crossref 44 hits), `hallucinated packages` (41 / 49), `slopsquatting` (5 / 5).
- Ranking is by novelty × laptop feasibility × impact, given the user's constraints (beginner, laptop only, no GPU, short project).
- Labels: [V] verified in the paper's data, [A] author claim, [I] our interpretation.

## Summary ranking

| Rank | Gap | Type | Confidence | Feasibility | Est. cost / time |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| G1 | How often coding agents *actually attempt to install* non-existent or suspicious packages in ordinary, non-adversarial tasks, and what they do after the install fails | population/context, evidence | medium | moderate | ≤ $100 API + 20–50 h unattended local runs; 4–6 weeks |
| G2 | No independent, shared-benchmark evaluation of laptop-runnable client-side pre-install guards on the hard cases (import≠distribution names, registered lookalikes, new legitimate packages, post-cutoff registrations) | practical, methodological | medium | easy–moderate | $0 API; 2–3 weeks |
| G3 | No validated, shared measurement protocol; the papers' decision rules disagree, so their rates and contradictions cannot be compared | methodological, contradiction | medium-high | easy | $5–30 API; 3–4 weeks incl. annotation |
| G4 | The effect of quantization *as deployed in local runtimes* (GGUF levels via Ollama) on spontaneous PyPI/npm package hallucination | population/context | medium-low | moderate (CPU time) | $0; 40–80 h unattended |
| G5 | Independent long-horizon (≥12-month) re-check of published hallucinated-name corpora for registration and weaponisation | evidence | low (largely narrowed by a new TOSEM paper) | easy | $0; 1 day + monthly cron |

---

## G1: We found no study that measures how often autonomous coding agents *actually run* `pip`/`npm install` on non-existent or suspicious package names during ordinary, non-adversarial tasks, or what they do after the install fails

- **Gap type:** population/context (agentic setting untested) + evidence (no base rate).

- **Evidence that the gap exists:**
  - The agentic setting is explicitly out of scope or named as future work in five independent analysed papers:
    - [A] Churilov states that agentic setups are not studied [@churilov2026range, p. 14].
    - [A] Dasu does not evaluate closed frontier models or agentic settings [@dasu2026refusing, p. 10].
    - [A] Twist names agentic coding workflows as future work [@twist2026library, p. 9].
    - [A] PackMonitor does not cover coding-agent workflows, `requirements.txt`, Dockerfiles or CI [@liu2026packmonitor, p. 19].
    - [A] Okwor proposes moving from self-generated output to live coding-agent traffic [@okwor2026hallucination, p. 8].
  - Installation itself is the harmful event, so measuring generated text alone misses the point:
    - [V] 56% of real malicious packages execute at install time, PyPI 96% [@ohm2020backstabbers, p. 8].
    - [V] Install-time execution through `setup.py` and npm `postinstall` was confirmed offline [@okwor2026hallucination, p. 7].
  - No paper reports actual installs. Measurement stops at generated text or is proxied by HTTP reachability:
    - [A] Haque calls for verifying by executing `go get` [@haque2025secure, p. 7].
    - [A] Zheng did not measure Cargo-level installation [@zheng2026when, p. 10].
  - Agent-like behaviours are suggestive but untested in agents:
    - [V] Models emit install commands even for names their own comments mark as placeholders [@zhao2025hfuzzer, p. 9].
    - [V] An optional PyPI-existence tool is rarely called by GPT-5-mini (7.89%), and invalid libraries remain in up to 38.79% of cases [@twist2026library, p. 8].
    - [V] Retry with a same-family fallback fails again on 83.5% of give-ups, and invented names recur across both models [@raj2026names, p. 10].
    - [I] What an agent does after a 404 (repeat, substitute a lookalike, or write its own code) is therefore an open and security-relevant question.
  - Persistence makes predictable agent installs plausible: [V] 43% of hallucinated names recur in 10 of 10 re-queries [@spracklen2024we, p. 9].
  - Independent support: five analysed papers from different groups list the agentic setting as untested, which makes this the most frequently stated gap in the set.

- **Novelty check (2026-11-12):**
  - `rlab search` queries (Crossref + arXiv, 2024– or 2025–):
    1. `coding agent installs hallucinated package pip npm` — OpenAlex failed (429); Crossref 25 hits; arXiv 0.
    2. `coding agent hallucinated package` — Crossref 24, arXiv 13.
    3. `slopsquatting agent` — Crossref 25, arXiv 1.
    4. `agent trajectories pip install dependency` — Crossref 24.
    5. `AI coding agent supply chain security dependencies` — Crossref 24, arXiv 8.
    6. `software engineering agent package installation security` — Crossref 24, arXiv 7.
    7. `hallucinated tool calls coding agents` — Crossref 24, arXiv 20.
    8. Plus the shared sweeps listed above.
  - WebSearch (2 queries) covered agent install measurement and SWE-agent/OpenHands trajectories. Two pages were also fetched with WebFetch (TrendAI report; DepScope post).
  - Closest hits and why they do not fill the gap:
    - **Bagmar & Saraf, "Setup Complete, Now You Are Compromised…" (arXiv 2607.15143).** [abstract] An *adversarial* evaluation: the attacker edits README, requirements or Makefile files, and the study tests production agent harnesses on 12 scenarios. It reports that a deterministic pre-install check closes most of the gap. Not a natural base rate with ordinary tasks and no attacker. Highly relevant: recommend for inclusion.
    - **Shan et al., "StateMirror…" (arXiv 2610.32648).** [abstract] A preliminary study of 4,398 agent trajectories finds "hallucinated tool use" to be pervasive, including actions on "missing packages". The mismatch is with the *local environment* (path or package not installed), not with the public registry. Slopsquatting exposure is not measured. Closest natural-trajectory evidence. Recommend for inclusion; read the full text to check whether registry-level non-existence is separable.
    - **TrendAI / Trend Micro report (S. Park, 2025-06-05, grey).** 100 web-dev tasks on foundation models. The 10 worst tasks were run manually on coding agents and Cursor with MCP. It reports counts of fabricated names (agents "approximately half"), does not say whether installs were executed, and gives no per-agent rates. Grey and small; not peer-reviewed.
    - **DepScope post (dev.to, grey, vendor).** Uses *induced* names supplied in the prompt and chat output only. "Installed" means "emitted an install command"; nothing was executed.
    - **SetupBench (arXiv 2507.09063)** and **Milliken et al., "Beyond pip Install" (SANER 2025, 10.1109/saner64311.2025.00009).** Agents bootstrapping environments; capability-focused, not slopsquatting. Useful as task sources.
    - **"Beyond Final Code" (arXiv 2503.12374, WebSearch only).** ModuleNotFoundError is common in SWE-bench agent logs. Environment errors, not registry checks.
    - Agent-attack papers in the project, not analysed (abstract-level only): arXiv 2610.09264 studies package-hallucination attacks on coding agents injected through rule files; arXiv 2605.29354 studies prompting attacks that steer hallucination through agent skills; arXiv 2605.09594 studies dependency steering through malicious agent skills. All three are *induced/adversarial* settings, not natural base rates.
  - Result: we found no study that measures executed package installs by coding agents on ordinary tasks against a live registry, or that characterises agent behaviour after a failed install (searches on 2026-11-12). The gap is narrowed from the scout version: adversarial agent installs and environment-level hallucinated tool calls are already studied.

- **Confidence: medium.**
  - For: five analysed papers state the gap, and two databases plus web search found only adversarial or environment-level neighbours.
  - Against: StateMirror's full text may contain registry-relevant counts. Vendor telemetry (e.g., Socket, Aikido) may exist unpublished. The field moves monthly.

- **Potential contribution:**
  1. The first natural base rate (with CIs) of agents attempting to install non-existent, post-cutoff or lookalike packages.
  2. A taxonomy of post-failure behaviour (correct fix / lookalike substitution / own implementation / give up / repeat).
  3. A direct agent-vs-chat comparison on the same tasks and model, testing whether the agent loop reduces or amplifies exposure.
  4. A reusable, *safe* measurement harness: a logging registry proxy that never executes unknown packages.

- **Suggested study (laptop-scale; benign tasks only):**
  - **Safety design (non-negotiable):**
    - Every run happens in a disposable Docker container or VM whose only network route is a **local logging package proxy**: devpi or a small PEP 503 simple-index proxy for PyPI, Verdaccio for npm.
    - The proxy forwards only names that exist and whose first release predates a fixed cutoff (e.g., 2026-01-01). Everything else gets a genuine 404 and is logged as "would-have-installed".
    - So no unknown or newly registered package code ever runs.
    - Never register any name. Report found names to PyPI/npm security through coordinated disclosure instead of publishing lists of unregistered names. [I] Churilov's publishing experiment was underpowered and cannot show that publishing is harmless [@churilov2026range, p. 12].
  - **Phase 0 (free, 1 week):**
    - Mine public agent-trajectory releases for `pip|uv|poetry|npm|yarn|pnpm add/install` commands. Example: SWE-bench submission trajectories; verify availability and licence first.
    - Score the names with the G3 protocol.
    - Gives an existing-data base rate. Caveat: SWE-bench environments are mostly pre-installed.
  - **Phase 1 (controlled runs):**
    - Agents:
      - Aider (open-source CLI; works with API models and Ollama);
      - mini-SWE-agent or OpenHands;
      - optionally Claude Code in headless mode, if the user has access.
    - Models:
      - one cheap frontier API model from Churilov's cohort (e.g., Claude Haiku 4.5 or GPT-5.4-mini);
      - one local model (qwen2.5-coder:7b, Ollama default quantization).
    - Tasks:
      - 200 Python tasks (optionally 100 JavaScript tasks) phrased neutrally ("Write and run a script that … Install whatever you need.");
      - converted from the public prompt corpus released with Spracklen/Churilov (39,969 prompts, [@churilov2026range, p. 4]);
      - stratified by Stack Overflow vs LLM-generated source and by topic recency, because both shift rates [@churilov2026range, p. 7; @spracklen2024we, pp. 8–9].
      - No fake names and no adversarial text in prompts.
    - 3 runs per task × agent × model (persistence).
    - **Baseline:** the same model in single-turn chat on the same task, scored with the same protocol.
  - **Metrics:**
    1. Per-task install-attempt hallucination rate: at least one install request for a name absent from the registry at run time. Report Wilson 95% CIs. With 0 events, use the rule-of-three upper bound.
    2. Per-install-command rate.
    3. Category shares: non-existent / import-name used as install name (e.g., `pip install cv2`) / registered lookalike / registered after model cutoff / correct.
    4. Post-404 behaviour distribution, including whether a substitute name is itself a low-reputation lookalike.
    5. Run-to-run persistence and Jaccard overlap of names across agents.
  - **Analysis:**
    - Paired agent-vs-chat comparison per task (McNemar);
    - logistic mixed model with a task random effect (agent, model, ecosystem, prompt source as fixed effects);
    - pre-register hypotheses and stopping rules.
  - **Sample-size reasoning:** if the true per-task rate is about 3%, 600 runs per configuration give about 18 events, a CI of roughly ±1.4 pp. Zero events bounds the rate below 0.5%, which is itself a publishable result.
  - **Cost and time:**
    - API agent runs use about 20k–100k tokens each, roughly $0.05–0.50 per run with a small model. Cap the API arm at 100 tasks × 3 runs, about ≤ $100.
    - Local Ollama arm: free, about 2–5 min per run on Apple Silicon, so about 20–50 h unattended.
    - Total 4–6 weeks.
  - **Expected threats to validity:**
    - low base rate (power);
    - proxy blocking alters downstream behaviour (mitigate: return a byte-identical registry 404);
    - agent and model version drift (log versions and dates);
    - task-selection bias towards install-heavy tasks [I], the same bias noted for Haque's GPT-4o filtering;
    - import-name ambiguity (handled by G3).

- **Feasibility for a beginner: moderate.**
  - Docker, a proxy and agent CLIs are well documented, and all scoring is offline Python.
  - The hard part is safe sandboxing and enough runs to get events. Phase 0 gives a no-risk start.

---

## G2: We found no independent evaluation, on a shared labelled benchmark, of laptop-runnable client-side pre-install guards on the cases that defeat a plain existence check

- **Gap type:** practical + methodological.

- **Evidence that the gap exists:**
  - Existence checks are necessary but not sufficient (stated by several papers):
    - [A] Plain registry checks are inadequate because attackers can pre-register names [@spracklen2024we, p. 12].
    - [I] Any registry-present name passes PackMonitor's mask, and vetted allowlists are not evaluated [@liu2026packmonitor, p. 6; @liu2026packmonitor, p. 19].
    - [A] If attackers pre-register hallucinated names, a registry oracle labels them valid (oracle poisoning) [@spracklen2026llm, p. 12].
  - The hard cases are real:
    - [V] 25 of 2,282 hallucinated names were registered within about six months, and at least 23 suggested names previously hosted malware [@churilov2026range, p. 12].
    - [V] 19 of 22 registered public names are placeholders [@okwor2026hallucination, pp. 5–6], and [A] a placeholder can be weaponised in a later release [@okwor2026hallucination, p. 8].
    - [V] Import names of real packages were the largest false-positive class (144–207 mentions per model) [@churilov2026range, p. 10].
  - Proposed but **not evaluated** defences:
    - [A] a date-aware verification list [@krishna2025importing, p. 8];
    - [A] registry grounding at generation time [@dasu2026refusing, p. 9];
    - [A] guided decoding plus lightweight registry verification [@djire2026evaluating, p. 11];
    - [A] a namespace- and near-miss-aware Rust guardrail [@zheng2026when, p. 9].
  - The only black-box guard in the set has known false-positive and drift problems:

# Research questions — Package Hallucination and Slopsquatting in LLM Coding Assistants: Measuring Hallucinated Dependencies, Their Exploitability on PyPI/npm, and Lightweight Defences

<!-- 3-5 questions. Each must be answerable from literature evidence. -->

## RQ1: How often do LLMs and coding agents hallucinate package names, and how does the rate vary by model, programming language/ecosystem, prompt type, quantization and agentic setting?
- Type: descriptive
- Why it matters: Base rate and drivers define the size of the threat and where to measure.
- Linked objective: O1
- Status: answered (literature)
- Current answer: Package hallucination appears in every model tested, from 2023–24 open models to 2026 frontier models, and in Python, JavaScript, Rust and Go [@spracklen2024we, p. 7; @churilov2026range, p. 6; @zheng2026when, p. 5; @haque2025secure, p. 6]. Its size depends on the unit and the model class: 3.63–5.02% of package mentions for five 2026 frontier models (preprint) [@churilov2026range, p. 6], against 16.1–47.9% of packages for small open 1–8B models [@djire2026evaluating, p. 5]. The best-supported drivers are the model itself and the prompt: year-based requests and user-supplied typos or fake names push rates very high [@twist2026library, p. 5; @twist2026library, p. 6]. Effects of language, size, temperature and quantization are contested or rest on one study [@haque2025secure, p. 6], and agentic settings have not been measured [@churilov2026range, p. 14]. Strength: moderate that it is non-zero and model-dependent; weak for most drivers.

## RQ2: What makes hallucinated packages exploitable: are names repeated across runs and models, do they collide with registered or malicious packages, and is there evidence of real-world slopsquatting?
- Type: descriptive
- Why it matters: Only persistent, predictable names are worth squatting; this defines the attack model.
- Linked objective: O2
- Status: answered (literature)
- Current answer: Hallucinated names are predictable enough to squat. 43% recur in all 10 re-queries [@spracklen2024we, p. 9], and 104 names are shared by all five 2026 frontier models, 54 of them one edit from a registered package [@churilov2026range, p. 9]. Real-world registration has so far been rare: 25 of 2,282 names in about six months, one of them with malware [@churilov2026range, p. 12], and publicly listed names are claimed mostly by defenders [@okwor2026hallucination, p. 5]. Install-time code execution, the payload route, is well documented [@ohm2020backstabbers, p. 8]. Strength: moderate for persistence; weak for real-world exploitation (two preprints, short observation windows).

## RQ3: Which defences against package hallucination have been proposed (fine-tuning, model editing, unlearning, RAG/self-check, registry-side checks), and how effective, costly and deployable are they?
- Type: comparative
- Why it matters: A beginner implementation study needs a cheap defence that works on ordinary hardware.
- Linked objective: O3
- Status: answered (literature)
- Current answer: White-box defences give the largest reductions: decoding-time logit masking (0% against its own list, ×1.07–×1.28 latency) [@liu2026packmonitor, p. 13; @liu2026packmonitor, p. 14], model editing [@liu2026mitigating, p. 7] and unlearning [@spracklen2026llm, p. 10]. All of them need weights or logits and were run on data-centre GPUs. Black-box options are cheap but inconsistent. RAG helps in some ecosystems and hurts in others [@djire2026evaluating, p. 6]. Greedy decoding is the best simple trade-off for small models [@djire2026evaluating, p. 8]. Self-check prompts and a PyPI tool reduce hallucination without removing it [@twist2026library, p. 18; @twist2026library, p. 21]. A registry existence check alone cannot catch names that are already squatted [@spracklen2024we, p. 12], and the only tool-side guard evaluation is weak [@raj2026names, p. 7]. Strength: weak to moderate (single runs, selected prompt sets, no independent replication).

## RQ4: How do studies measure package hallucination (prompt sources, ground-truth registry snapshots, metrics, deduplication), and what methodological weaknesses threaten their validity?
- Type: methodological
- Why it matters: A new measurement must avoid known pitfalls (stale registry snapshots, name normalisation, contamination).
- Linked objective: O4
- Status: answered (literature)
- Current answer: Studies differ in prompt source, extraction method (install commands, model-queried lists or import parsing), existence rule (static vs live snapshot, release-date cutoff or none), stdlib and import-name handling, and the unit of the rate. Because of this, rates cannot be pooled or ranked across papers [@spracklen2024we, p. 6; @krishna2025importing, p. 4; @churilov2026range, p. 5]. The largest documented biases are counting stdlib modules (+7.6 to +9.4 pp in Python) [@djire2026evaluating, p. 5] and counting import names of real packages, which were the largest false-positive class; the live re-check lowered rates by about a fifth [@churilov2026range, p. 10]. Further threats are pseudo-replicated statistics [@krishna2025importing, p. 6], quantization confounds [@dasu2026refusing, p. 10], and labelling compliance with planted names as invention [@twist2026library, p. 6]. Strength: moderate.

## RQ5: What has not yet been tested — e.g. agentic tools that install dependencies automatically, newer models, other ecosystems, lightweight client-side defences — that a laptop-scale study could address?
- Type: methodological
- Why it matters: Directly yields the implementation project (answered via gap report + novelty check).
- Linked objective: O4
- Status: partially answered
- Current answer: the analysed papers do not test agentic tools that install dependencies on their own [@churilov2026range, p. 14; @dasu2026refusing, p. 10; @liu2026packmonitor, p. 19]. They also leave three other areas untested: local quantized models in PyPI/npm settings [@churilov2026range, p. 14]; client-side guards that run on ordinary hardware and look beyond plain existence [@raj2026names, p. 13]; and a shared live, dated, mapping- and stdlib-aware measurement protocol. Only static analysis has been run on a laptop-class machine [@mirandapena2026empirical, p. 17]. Three agent-side attack papers in the project are still unanalysed and must be read before an agent-related gap is claimed. Strength: preliminary; none of these is a confirmed gap until gap-report.md records a novelty check.

## Speed at the Cost of Quality: How Cursor AI Increases Short-Term Velocity and Long-Term Complexity in Open-Source Projects
> **Takeaway:** In real open-source projects, adopting the agentic coding tool Cursor gave a short burst of extra code, while code complexity rose and stayed higher. The quality result is not robust to every statistical method, so treat it as strong-but-contested evidence, not settled fact.

| Item | Detail |
|---|---|
| Authors | Hao He, Courtney Miller, Shyam Agarwal, Christian Kästner, Bogdan Vasilescu |
| Year · Venue | 2026 · Proceedings of the 23rd International Conference on Mining Software Repositories (MSR 2026) |
| Status | Peer-reviewed. Our copy is the arXiv v3 version (with appendices), so page numbers follow that copy |
| Identifier | DOI 10.1145/3793302.3793349 (arXiv 2511.04427) |
| Paper type | Empirical study (quasi-experimental causal analysis of GitHub repository data) |
| Relevance to us | High — RQ3 (main), RQ4, RQ5 |

### In plain words
Many developers now use AI coding agents that can edit many files on their own. People claim these tools make teams faster, but nobody knew whether that speed lasts or whether the code gets worse. The authors looked at real open-source projects on GitHub that started using Cursor, an AI-powered code editor with an "agent" mode that can plan, edit and debug code with the human mainly supervising [@he2026speed, p. 3]. They compared these projects with similar projects that did not adopt Cursor, month by month. This matters because if AI speed is bought with harder-to-maintain code, the speed may not pay off later.

### How they did it
1. Find adopters. They searched GitHub for Cursor configuration files (such as .cursorrules). The first commit of such a file counts as the moment a project "adopted" Cursor [@he2026speed, p. 4].
2. Find look-alike controls. For each adopter they picked similar projects that never adopted Cursor, using propensity-score matching (a statistical way to find projects with a similar history of activity, size and popularity) [@he2026speed, p. 4; @he2026speed, p. 5].
3. Measure every month. For each project and month they counted commits and lines added (speed), and ran SonarQube (a widely used code-checking tool) to get static-analysis warnings, code duplication and cognitive complexity (a score for how hard code is to understand) [@he2026speed, p. 5].
4. Compare before and after. They used difference-in-differences (comparing how adopters changed over time against how controls changed, so shared trends cancel out). The main version is the Borusyak imputation estimator, chosen because simpler methods can be biased when projects adopt at different times [@he2026speed, p. 6].
5. Test how speed and quality feed into each other. A second model (Arellano-Bond dynamic panel, a method for data where this month depends on last month) checked whether more complexity or warnings slow down later work [@he2026speed, p. 6; @he2026speed, p. 8].
6. Robustness checks. They re-ran the analysis with two other estimators and on many subsets [@he2026speed, p. 9; @he2026speed, p. 16].

### Data and setup
- 806 GitHub projects with at least 10 stars that adopted Cursor, with adoption dates between Jan 2024 and Mar 2025 and most adoptions between Aug 2024 and Mar 2025 [@he2026speed, p. 2; @he2026speed, p. 4].
- 1,380 matched control projects in the text; a table lists 801 treated and 1,172 control projects with 21,699 project-months [@he2026speed, p. 2; @he2026speed, p. 17]. The paper does not explain the difference.
- Monthly data from Jan 2024 to Aug 2025 [@he2026speed, p. 5].
- Main languages: TypeScript 366, Python 118, JavaScript 60, Go 36, Rust 24 projects [@he2026speed, p. 4].
- The comparison is against "current practice", not against no AI: controls may use Copilot or ChatGPT without leaving traces [@he2026speed, p. 7].
- Replication package on Zenodo [@he2026speed, p. 11].

### Key findings
- [V] Overall, lines added rose by +28.58% and commits by +2.63% (not significant) [@he2026speed, p. 7].
- [V] The speed boost is short-lived: lines added +281.3% in month 1 and +48.4% in month 2, then no significant effect [@he2026speed, p. 8].
- [V] With the main estimator, static-analysis warnings rose by +30.26% and code complexity by +41.64% (both p < 0.001); duplication +7.03% was not significant [@he2026speed, p. 7].
- [V] These quality effects depend on the estimator. Another method (Callaway–Sant'Anna) gives negative, non-significant results: warnings −10.49%, complexity −3.80%. The authors say the quality findings need caution [@he2026speed, p. 16].
- [V] Once codebase size is controlled, Cursor has no significant direct effect on warnings, but it still raises complexity (coefficient 0.086, p < 0.01) [@he2026speed, p. 8].
- [V] More complexity and warnings go with slower later work: a 100% rise in complexity or warnings goes with a 64.5% or 50.3% drop in next-month lines added [@he2026speed, p. 8].
- [A] The authors read the warning rise as mostly "more code, more warnings", while complexity is inherently higher in Cursor code [@he2026speed, p. 10].

### Limitations and weaknesses
- [A] Only projects that commit Cursor files are seen, and how much they really used Cursor is unknown. The results are "intent-to-treat" (the effect of adopting, not of using heavily) [@he2026speed, p. 7].
- [A] Unmeasured differences (team skill, practices) may remain despite matching [@he2026speed, p. 7].
- [A] The quality metrics may miss aspects of quality, and complexity metrics were designed for human code [@he2026speed, p. 11].
- [I] Warnings and complexity are totals for the whole project, so they grow with project size. "+30% warnings" mainly means "more code", not more warnings per line (based on [@he2026speed, p. 8]).
- [I] The abstract does not mention the estimator sensitivity reported in the appendix [@he2026speed, p. 16].
- [I] Some numbers are inconsistent: the discussion cites a 25.1% complexity rise, while the tables report +41.64% and a coefficient of about 9% [@he2026speed, p. 10; @he2026speed, p. 7; @he2026speed, p. 8]. Use the table values.
- [I] Quality is measured by static analysis only; no tests or functional correctness are measured.

### Gaps and future work this paper leaves open
- [A] Replicate with other and newer AI tools, in company (enterprise) settings and in more languages [@he2026speed, p. 7; @he2026speed, p. 11; @he2026speed, p. 16].
- [A] Find out why AI tools produce overly complex code [@he2026speed, p. 11].
- [I] G1: it does not study rebuilding an app from its interface or behaviour. A reconstruction study still has to measure fidelity and maintainability together.
- [I] G3: its quality story changes with the measuring method, which supports checking whether quality tools agree for AI-built apps.

### Why it matters for your research
This is the strongest real-world causal evidence in our set that agent-style coding can raise code complexity. It does not study reconstruction, so it informs your quality question (RQ3) by analogy only. Reuse its metric set: SonarQube warnings, cognitive complexity and duplication. Avoid its main weakness: always normalise counts by code size (for example per 1,000 lines), and check results with more than one method. When you quote "+30% warnings / +41.6% complexity", always add that they are estimator-sensitive.

### Connections to other papers
- [V] Contrasts with borg2026echoes: a randomised experiment found no significant difference when a second developer evolved AI-assisted code [@borg2026echoes, p. 33; @borg2026echoes, p. 38]. Our evidence matrix treats the two as not necessarily in conflict (contradiction C1).
- [A] ehsani2026faster repeats this paper's +30% / +41% figures without the caveats; count the effect once, from this paper [@ehsani2026faster, p. 18].
- [V] Consistent with the idea that AI adds code volume: AI-assisted outliers of up to 10,788 lines in borg2026echoes [@borg2026echoes, p. 30], and architectural smells that track code size in zhu2026understanding [@zhu2026understanding, p. 8].
- [V] Uses a different meaning of "vibe coding" from fawzy2026vibe [@fawzy2026vibe, p. 1], so results should not be pooled (C9).

# PackMonitor: Towards Zero Package Hallucinations via Decoding-Time Monitoring

- Authors: Liu, Xiting; Liu, Yuetong; Zhang, Yitong; Li, Jia; Hu, Shi-Min
- Year / venue: 2026, Proceedings of the ACM on Software Engineering (published)
- DOI: 10.1145/3832118 · URL: https://doi.org/10.1145/3832118
- Source text: `fulltext.txt` (page refs = PDF page index)

Labels: **[V]** verified in the paper's own data/tables/results · **[A]** author claim · **[I]** our interpretation.

Source tier: peer-reviewed (PACMSE, ISSTA 2026 issue, article ISSTA027) (p. 1). The text used is arXiv v2, whose first page carries the ACM DOI and publication data (p. 1).

## 1. Research objective
- [A] Eliminate package hallucinations in LLM dependency recommendations, not merely reduce them. The argument: package-name validity can be decided against a finite, enumerable authoritative package list, so hallucinated names can be made unreachable during decoding (p. 1, p. 2).
- [A] Achieve this without training, as a plug-in, with low latency and no loss of model utility (p. 1, p. 3).

## 2. Research questions / hypotheses
- [V] RQ1: How effective is PackMonitor at eliminating package hallucinations compared with baselines? (p. 10)
- [V] RQ2: How much efficiency overhead does it add? (p. 10)
- [V] RQ3: Does it degrade general code-generation capability? (p. 10)
- [V] RQ4: How much does DFA caching improve inference efficiency and scalability? (p. 10)

## 3. Methodology
- Research design: [V] A technique proposal tested by controlled comparison against training-free baselines (RAG, Self-Refinement, RAG+SR) on HFuzzer and against SFT on Package4U. It also includes an ablation (with vs without cache) and a scaling test of DFA construction and loading time (p. 10, p. 12–17).
- Approach / model / intervention:
  - [V] A *Context-Aware Parser*, modelled on a context-free grammar, tracks whether the output is natural language, an ordinary code line, or the package names of an installation command. It recognises code blocks by delimiters such as ```bash and switches intervention on only after `pip install` (grammar `INSTALL_CMD_LINE → pip install PACKAGE_NAMES \n`) (p. 8).
  - [V] A *Package-Name Intervenor* compiles the authoritative list into a deterministic finite automaton (DFA, a state machine that accepts exactly the listed names). A token trie is built from the tokenizer vocabulary. At each step, every token that cannot extend the current prefix towards some allowlisted name gets logit −∞. A terminator is allowed only once the prefix is a complete allowlisted name (p. 6, p. 8–9).
  - [V] A *DFA-Caching Mechanism* builds the DFA once offline, stores it as a checkpoint and loads it at inference time (p. 10).
  - [V] **Required access:** the method masks the model's logits at every decoding step, so it needs next-token logits from a locally decoded model plus that model's tokenizer vocabulary (p. 9). No training and no weight changes (p. 3).
  - [I] It therefore cannot be added to a closed chat API (ChatGPT, Claude, Copilot) that does not expose per-step logits or accept an arbitrary token-level constraint. The paper does not discuss black-box APIs.
- Baselines or comparison conditions:
  - [V] Vanilla; RAG (retrieved valid package names injected into the prompt); Self-Refinement (SR); RAG+SR; and SFT, using the fine-tuned checkpoints released by Spracklen et al. (p. 11, p. 13–14).
  - [V] "Following prior work on mitigating package hallucinations [41], we include three representative baselines" (p. 11). The RAG retriever, corpus and k are not reported.
  - [I] No baseline is a simple post-generation registry lookup that blocks invalid names.

## 4. Dataset and sample
- Data source(s):
  - [V] HFuzzer (Zhao et al., ASE 2025) is the primary evaluation framework. It is a fuzzer in which a tester model (DeepSeek-V3, temperature 0) iteratively writes test cases for the target model (temperature 0.7) (p. 10–12).
  - [V] Package4U, the ~40,000-task dataset of Spracklen et al. (about half Python), is used "in a subset of our experiments", namely the SFT comparison (p. 11, p. 14).
  - [V] HumanEval is used for utility (p. 16).
  - [V] Authoritative list: the PyPI index, 706,618 names "at the time of our experiments", obtained via PyPI's official API (p. 12, p. 19). The snapshot date is not reported.
- Sample size (N) and unit:
  - [V] Five open-weight models: DeepSeek-Coder-Instruct-6.7B, CodeLlama-7b-Instruct, Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct, Meta-Llama-3-8B-Instruct and Meta-Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (p. 11).
  - [V] One HFuzzer round of 1,000 iterations per model × configuration (p. 12).
  - [V] Units are recommended packages (P_total from 231 to 2,288 per run) and responses (Table 2, p. 13).
  - The Package4U subset size is not reported.
- Sampling / selection method: [V] Models follow HFuzzer's selection "to ensure a fair comparison" (p. 11). HFuzzer generates prompts adaptively (p. 10). [I] So each configuration sees a different, self-generated prompt stream.
- Data availability (public? link?): [V] Code is at https://github.com/THU-Agent/PackMonitor (p. 20). Settings are in the supplementary material (p. 19). Release of HFuzzer transcripts: not reported.

## 5. Experimental setup
- Procedure, settings, hyper-parameters, tools:
  - [V] Tester temperature 0 and target temperature 0.7 on HFuzzer; temperature 0 for HumanEval (p. 12, p. 16).
  - [V] **Hallucination decision:**
    - The definition covers non-existent packages and packages from the wrong ecosystem (p. 2, p. 4).
    - Validity is membership of "a finite and enumerable list of valid package names … either from an official registry snapshot or a curated allowlist" (p. 6). In the experiments that list is the PyPI index (p. 12).
    - The metrics (PHR, RHR, unique count) are adopted from Spracklen et al. and HFuzzer (p. 12).
    - [I] Whether HFuzzer's own oracle uses the same 706,618-name list is not stated. If it does, the 0% result holds by construction.
  - [I] **Import path vs install name.** The paper's own motivating example is import-path vs install-name confusion: `google.protobuf` is a legitimate import path, but `google-protobuf` is not in the list (p. 6). The mask guarantees only that *some* listed name is produced, not the intended package.
  - **Stdlib handling:** not reported. [I] This matters little here, because only `pip install` arguments are constrained and scored.
  - **Name normalisation** (case, `-`/`_`): not reported.
  - Handling of version pins, flags (`-U`, `-r`), `python -m pip` and `conda`/`npm`: not reported for the experiments. Other ecosystems are discussed only "in principle" (p. 19).
  - [V] **Hardware:** a server with 8× NVIDIA A100 80 GB, 2× AMD EPYC 7543 (64 cores) and 1 TB RAM, running Ubuntu 22.04 (p. 12). GPUs used per run, inference framework and DFA memory footprint: not reported.
  - [V] **Overhead, with cache:** time per response rises ×1.07–×1.28, i.e. +0.06 s to +0.58 s (Table 4, p. 14). The text says "around 0.2s in the worst case" (p. 15), but CodeLlama goes from 2.4296 s to 3.0130 s (+0.58 s) (p. 14).
  - [V] **Overhead, without cache:** ×2.81–×6.24 (Table 6, p. 17).
  - [V] **DFA build vs load:** building takes 0.021 s (7k names), 4.407 s (700k) and 21.121 s (3,000k); loading takes 0.002–0.247 s (Table 7, p. 17).
- Code availability: [V] Public GitHub repository (p. 20).

## 6. Evaluation metrics
- Metric — what it measures — why chosen:
  - [V] PHR is hallucinated packages divided by recommended packages. RHR is the share of responses with at least one hallucinated package. P_hall-unique counts distinct hallucinated names, as a measure of diversity. All three are adopted from prior work (p. 12).
  - [V] P_total checks that the method does not work by suppressing recommendations (p. 13).
  - [V] Mean generation time measures overhead (p. 15). HumanEval Pass@1 measures utility (p. 16).
  - [I] There is no metric of whether the forced package is correct or relevant for the task (cf. Package Utility in djire2026evaluating).
- Statistical testing: [V] None. Single runs. Only Fig. 3 shows a standard deviation of latency (p. 15).

## 7. Key findings
1. [V] PHR and RHR are 0% on all five models on HFuzzer. For example, DeepSeek-Coder goes from 8.39% / 11.60% (vanilla) to 0% / 0% (Table 2, p. 13). The lowest baseline is RAG+SR on CodeLlama at 1.30% PHR, but that run produced only 231 recommended packages vs 1,004 for vanilla (p. 13).
2. [V] RAG can increase hallucination. Qwen2.5-Coder PHR goes from 3.25% to 3.33%, and Llama-3 RHR from 6.40% to 7.10% (p. 12–13). SR never reaches zero; DeepSeek-Coder ends at 7.55% PHR (p. 13).
3. [V] On Package4U, SFT lowers PHR from 16.14% to 2.66% (DeepSeek-Coder) and from 26.28% to 10.27% (CodeLlama); PackMonitor gives 0% (Table 3, p. 14). The SFT checkpoints could not run through HFuzzer because their instruction-following was degraded (p. 14).
4. [V] Overhead with cache is ×1.07–×1.28, against RAG up to ×1.70, SR up to ×1.94 and RAG+SR up to ×2.65 (Table 4, p. 14–15).
5. [V] HumanEval Pass@1 is unchanged on all five models (e.g. 72.6% vs 72.6%). The SFT drops of −26.9 and −14.0 pp are quoted from [41], not re-measured (Table 5, p. 16).
6. [V] P_total is described as "comparable", e.g. DeepSeek-Coder 1,847 vs 1,648. But CodeLlama goes from 1,004 to 1,514 (p. 13).

## 8. Limitations stated by the authors
- [A] The guarantee is conditional on the correctness and completeness of the list. A stale snapshot or omissions undermine it, so the list must be refreshed periodically (p. 18–19).
- [A] Timing results may vary with deployment hardware. Effectiveness does not (p. 19).
- [A] Scope is chat-based PyPI recommendations after `pip install` only. It does not cover `requirements.txt`, Dockerfiles, CI configurations or coding-agent workflows (p. 19).
- [A] It targets name validity, not executability, API compatibility or version compatibility (p. 19).
- [A] Generalisability across models is argued from five LLMs plus adversarial HFuzzer prompts (p. 19).

## 9. Limitations we identified
- [I] **0% is largely by construction.** If PHR is scored against the enforced list, the informative results are only overhead, P_total and utility.
- [I] **"Valid" ≠ safe.** Any name on PyPI passes, including hallucinated names already squatted by attackers, typosquats and malware that has not yet been removed. This is the core slopsquatting case (RQ2). Custom allowlists are mentioned (p. 6, p. 19) but not evaluated.
- [I] **Forced substitutions are unmeasured.** When the model would emit a non-existent name, the mask forces it onto some existing name sharing a prefix. That name may be wrong, or itself a squatted look-alike. There is no relevance metric. The paper's own `google-protobuf` example (p. 6) is exactly this import-name vs install-name case.
- [I] **Cross-ecosystem confusion is only partly covered.** The definition counts wrong-ecosystem packages as hallucinations (p. 2, p. 4), but the mask checks only PyPI membership. An npm name that also exists on PyPI (e.g. the paper's `jsonwebtoken` example, p. 2) would pass if registered there; whether it is registered is not reported.
- [I] **Prompt streams differ.** Adaptive fuzzing gives each configuration different prompts: CodeLlama P_total differs by 51% (1,004 vanilla vs 1,514 PackMonitor), and CodeLlama RAG+SR yields only 231 packages, so its 1.30% PHR rests on far fewer recommendations (p. 13). There is one round per configuration and no variance.
- [I] **The HumanEval test cannot reveal harm.** HumanEval contains almost no `pip install`, and decoding is greedy (p. 16), so the intervenor never fires.
- [I] **Narrow trigger surface.** `import` lines, requirements files, version pins and flags are not covered, so an agent writing `requirements.txt` bypasses the monitor.
- [I] **Some baseline numbers appear borrowed.** The Package4U vanilla figures (16.14%, 26.28%) equal those quoted from [41] (p. 4). It is unclear whether they were re-measured; cite spracklen2024we for them.
- [I] **No CPU measurement.** Overhead was measured on A100s only; the CPU cost of the trie/DFA intersection is unknown.

## 10. Threats to validity
- Internal (confounds, leakage, selection): [I] Adaptive prompt streams differ per configuration. The tester reacts to target outputs.
- External (generalisability of sample/context): [V] Five open 7–8B models, PyPI only, chat setting only (p. 11, p. 19). No API models, agents or npm.
- Construct (do metrics measure the concept?): [I] PHR is measured against the enforcement list itself. "Valid" means listed, not safe, intended or correct.
- Statistical conclusion (power, multiple comparisons, variance): [V] One round per configuration, no tests or confidence intervals (p. 12–13).
- Reproducibility (data/code/setup reported?): [V] Code, hardware and temperatures are given (p. 12, p. 20). Missing: snapshot date, normalisation, RAG configuration, Package4U subset.

## 11. Future research directions
- Stated by authors [A]:
  - Extend to `conda`/`npm` and to private allowlists (p. 19).
  - Cover requirements files, Dockerfiles, CI and agents (p. 19).
  - Address executability and version compatibility (p. 19–20).
  - Refresh the list periodically (p. 19).
- Suggested by us [I]:
  - Test a vetted allowlist (minimum package age or downloads).
  - Measure the relevance of forced substitutions.
  - Use a fixed prompt set across configurations.
  - Compare with a plain registry filter.
  - Measure CPU-only overhead.

## 12. Relevance to our research
- Research questions addressed (RQ ids): RQ3, RQ4, RQ5.
- How it informs our work [I]:
  - **Laptop feasibility:** it needs a locally decoded open-weight model exposing logits and tokenizer, and CPU-only operation is untested. All timings come from 8×A100 (p. 12, p. 19). DFA loading takes ≤0.25 s (p. 17), but that is host-side and does not show that 7–8B decoding is laptop-feasible. Not usable with closed APIs.
  - **What it leaves open:**
    - Names that already exist on the registry because an attacker registered them.
    - Correctness of forced substitutions.
    - Surfaces other than `pip install`.
    - npm and other ecosystems.
    - Black-box models.
  - **The cheap competitor:** a client-side registry or allowlist check gives the same "no non-existent name is installed" property without logit access. It is the natural low-compute comparison and was not tested.

## 13. Evidence table (for the evidence matrix)
| RQ | Claim | Page | Label | Strength |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| RQ3 | Decoding-time DFA logit masking against a PyPI list (706,618 names) yields 0% PHR/RHR on 5 open 7–8B models on HFuzzer, vs residual 1.30–7.55% PHR for RAG/SR/RAG+SR (1.30% on only 231 packages) | p. 12–13 | V | moderate |
| RQ3 | RAG can raise hallucination (Qwen2.5-Coder PHR 3.25%→3.33%; Llama-3 RHR 6.40%→7.10%) | p. 12–13 | V | weak |
| RQ3 | Overhead with cached DFA ×1.07–×1.28 per response (A100 server); ×2.81–×6.24 without cache | p. 14, p. 17 | V | moderate |
| RQ3 | HumanEval Pass@1 unchanged with PackMonitor on all 5 models (temperature 0) | p. 16 | V | weak |
| RQ3 | Requires per-step logits and tokenizer of a locally decoded model; training-free | p. 3, p. 9 | V | strong |
| RQ3 | SFT checkpoints still leave 2.66% / 10.27% PHR on Package4U (vanilla values as in spracklen2024we) | p. 14 | V | moderate |
| RQ4 | Guarantee conditional on correctness/completeness of the authoritative list; list must be refreshed | p. 18–19 | A | moderate |
| RQ4 | Mask guarantees some listed name, not the intended one (import path `google.protobuf` vs install name) | p. 6 | I | moderate |
| RQ2 | Any registry-present name passes the mask, so already-squatted names are not blocked (vetted allowlists not evaluated) | p. 6, p. 19 | I | moderate |
| RQ5 | Not evaluated: requirements.txt, Dockerfiles, CI configs, coding-agent workflows, non-PyPI ecosystems | p. 19 | A | strong |

## 14. Key quotes
> "this guarantee is conditional on the correctness and completeness of the given authoritative package list" (p. 18)

> "do not yet cover broader dependency specifications such as requirements.txt, Dockerfiles, CI configurations, or end-to-end coding-agent workflows" (p. 19)

> "This list comprises 706,618 valid package names at the time of our experiments" (p. 12)

## Analyst notes
- Reading coverage: all 23 PDF pages (pp. 20–23 are references). Tables 2–7 extracted cleanly. Fig. 3 is known only from the text.
- Metadata: `rlab validate` reports MISMATCH only because the arXiv listing title differs (similarity 0.854). Crossref and OpenAlex are verified (similarity 1.0), and the DOI is printed in the PDF (p. 1).
- Uncertainties:
  - Whether HFuzzer's oracle is the same list.
  - Whether the Package4U numbers were re-measured.
  - The Package4U subset size.
  - The worst-case overhead: the text says ~0.2 s, but Table 4 gives +0.58 s (p. 14–15).
- Funding: Chinese MoE, Tsinghua–Tencent lab, Tsinghua–Keystone centre, Beijing NSF (p. 20). No conflict of interest apparent.
- Review fixes (critical review 2026-11-12) applied while `ready`:
  - Verbatim baseline quote.
  - Hallucination-definition pages.
  - Import-name caveat.
  - Laptop-feasibility wording.
  - RAG+SR package count.
  - Validate note.
