# Evaluating Inference-Time Defenses against Package Hallucination in LLM-Generated Code

- Authors: Djire, Alberick Euraste; Olatunji, Iyiola E.; Tessa, Melissa; Barr, Earl T.; Klein, Jacques; Bissyandé, Tegawendé F.
- Year / venue: 2026, Proceedings of the 41st IEEE/ACM International Conference on Automated Software Engineering (published)
- DOI: 10.1145/3832783.3837555 · URL: https://doi.org/10.1145/3832783.3837555
- Source text: `fulltext.txt` (page refs = PDF page index)

Labels: **[V]** verified · **[A]** author claim · **[I]** our interpretation.

Source tier: peer-reviewed (ASE 2026) (p. 1). The text used is arXiv v1, which carries the ACM DOI (p. 1).

## 1. Research objective
- [A] Four contributions (p. 1–2):
  - Correct registry-based measurement, which misclassifies standard-library modules as hallucinations.
  - Evaluate seven inference-time defences.
  - Introduce a Package Utility (PU) metric.
  - Stress-test the defences with adversarial prompts.
- [A] The focus is small open models, because they hallucinate more and run on resource-constrained hardware (p. 2, p. 4).

## 2. Research questions / hypotheses
- [V] RQ1: How does baseline PHR vary across model families and languages once stdlib imports are accounted for?
- [V] RQ2: How effective is guided decoding compared with RAG and Self-Refine?
- [V] RQ3: What is the trade-off between mitigation and utility?
- [V] RQ4: How robust are the defences to prompts seeded with fabricated names? (p. 3)

## 3. Methodology
- Research design: [V] Factorial comparison: 8 models × 4 languages (Python, JavaScript, Ruby, Rust) × vanilla + 7 strategies. Each runs on the full D_eval with 3 independent runs (p. 3, p. 5).
- Approach / model / intervention (with **required access**):
  - [V] **Greedy:** T=0 (p. 5). The paper counts Greedy as one of its five guided decoding strategies (p. 2, p. 6). [I] Works with an API.
  - [V] **Contrastive Decoding (CD):** α=0.5, "amateur/expert layer pairing (model-specific)" (Table 1, p. 5). The text describes subtracting a smaller amateur model's log-probabilities (p. 4). [I] It needs logits from two models (or layers); the description is inconsistent.
  - [V] **DoLa:** contrasts the final layer with early layers {4, 8, 12, 16}; repetition penalty 1.2 (p. 5). [I] White-box: needs intermediate hidden states.
  - [V] **ALCD:** DoLa plus an entropy ≥1 activation policy (p. 5). [I] White-box.
  - [V] **Nudging:** the surrogate is the "largest in family"; top-probability threshold 0.4 (p. 5). [I] Needs token probabilities plus a second model. Given the model list (p. 3), the largest in family is the model itself for 5 of 8 models (gemma-4b, deepseek-6.7b, qwen-3b, mistral-7b, llama-8b). The paper does not explain what Nudging does in those cases (p. 5).
  - [V] **Self-Refine:** up to 5 iterations of self-critique (p. 4–5). [I] Black-box. Whether the critique sees registry data is not reported.
  - [V] **RAG:** retrieval k=5 over a per-language registry corpus, following Spracklen et al.'s top-k setup (p. 4–5). Retriever and embedder: not reported. [I] Black-box model plus an external index.
  - [A] CD and Nudging run two models at once, so model sizes were capped to fit one GPU (p. 4).
- Baselines or comparison conditions: [V] Vanilla decoding with T=1.0, top-k 50, top-p 1.0 (p. 4–5). One fixed configuration per strategy, based on Shi et al. (p. 4).

## 4. Dataset and sample
- Data source(s):
  - [V] Step 1: the top 1,000 most popular packages per registry via the Libraries.io API, as (name, description) pairs (p. 3).
  - [V] Step 2: full registry name lists "as of March 4, 2026", plus standard-library module lists. The ground truth P_ℓ is registry ∪ stdlib (p. 3).
  - [V] Step 3: GPT-4o-mini writes one coding instruction per pair. The system prompt asks for a bracketed package list (p. 3).
- Sample size (N) and unit:
  - [V] D_eval has 4,000 instructions, 1,000 per language (p. 3).
  - [V] Eight models: gemma-1b/4b, deepseek-coder-1.3b/6.7b, qwen2.5-1.5b/3b, mistral-7b-Instruct-v0.3, llama-3.1-8b (p. 3).
  - [V] Generated packages range from 1,470 to 32,337 per model–language cell under vanilla decoding (Table 3, p. 6).
- Sampling / selection method:
  - [V] Adversarial set: 1,000 non-existent names each for Python and JavaScript, produced by Meta-Llama, Alibaba and OpenAI GPT models, verified absent from npm/PyPI by direct lookup. The same names are reused as seeds for Ruby and Rust and placed into "install and use" templates, giving 4,000 prompts (p. 9).
  - [V] Code-generation extension: the same instructions, asking for runnable code; imports are validated against the same snapshots (p. 6).
- Data availability (public? link?): [V] Code, datasets and instructions on Zenodo record 21786704 (p. 11).

## 5. Experimental setup
- Procedure, settings, hyper-parameters, tools:
  - [V] **Hallucination decision:** a name is "classified as hallucinated if and only if it is absent from P_ℓ" (p. 4).
  - Not reported: name normalisation and output-parser details.
  - [V] **Code generation:** "All imported packages are validated against the same registry snapshots" (p. 6). No import-to-distribution mapping is described.
    - [I] Import names that are not registered under the same name (e.g. `cv2` for `opencv-python`) probably count as hallucinations. That would inflate the hallucinated counts in Fig. 1.
  - [V] **Stdlib:** manifests were collected for "the two applicable languages" (Python, Ruby) (p. 5), although Step 2 says every snapshot is augmented (p. 3). [I] Treatment of JavaScript and Rust built-ins is unclear.
  - [V] **Hardware:** "within the memory budget of a single GPU" (p. 4). GPU type, inference library and runtimes: not reported.
  - **Overhead/latency of the strategies:** not reported.
  - [V] **Code quality:** Semgrep syntax-error rate and code-smell count (p. 7).
  - [V] Mean ± SD over 3 runs; per-run values are in the artifact (p. 5).
- Code availability: [V] Zenodo (p. 11).

## 6. Evaluation metrics
- Metric — what it measures — why chosen:
  - [V] Micro-PHR pools all generated names. Macro-PHR averages per prompt, and a prompt with no output counts as 0 (p. 4). [I] Macro-PHR therefore rewards silence.
  - [V] PU is the F1 of precision and recall against R_i: the seed package plus the k−1 packages with most similar descriptions (text-embedding-3-small, cosine), k ∈ {1, 2, 5, 10}, plus a reference set derived from generated code. PU is 0 for empty outputs (p. 4, p. 7). [A] PU "remains a semantic proxy" (p. 4).
  - [V] Syntax-error rate and mean smell count (p. 7–8).
- Statistical testing: [V] Mean ± SD over 3 runs. No significance tests or confidence intervals. Counts like "19 of 32" are not corrected for multiple comparisons (p. 5–10).

## 7. Key findings
1. [V] **Stdlib correction:** pooled Python vanilla PHR is 24.7% with stdlib vs 32.3% without (+7.6 pp). The maximum is +9.4 pp (Self-Refine); Ruby ranges +1.6 to +2.5 pp (Table 2, p. 5). [V] Table 3's Python counts sum to N_gen 79,965 and N_hall 19,776, which gives 24.7% (p. 6).
2. [V] **Baseline:** corrected vanilla micro-PHR ranges from 16.1% (Mistral-7b) to 47.9% (Qwen-1.5b) overall, peaks at 63.1% (Qwen-1.5b, Rust) and is lowest at 7.6% (Mistral, JavaScript). Larger in-family models cut PHR by 18.3–20.3 pp (p. 5–6).
3. [V] **Defences:**
   - RAG has the lowest PHR in 19 of 32 configurations and lowers the cross-model average from 29.7% to 18.1%. But it raises JavaScript PHR for 7 of 8 models, by 12.7 pp on average (p. 6).
   - By our count from Table 4, RAG is below Vanilla in 24 of 32 cells (p. 7).
   - Greedy matches Self-Refine at 25.6% average PHR (p. 6).
   - DoLa is the worst guided method at 38.0% overall, and 83.5–91.2% on DeepSeek-1.3b (p. 6).
   - CD never achieves the lowest PHR (p. 6), although by our count it is below Vanilla in 19 of 32 cells (Table 4, p. 7). ALCD mostly underperforms vanilla (p. 6–7).
4. [V] **Utility:** Greedy gives the best trade-off, with the highest PU under all five reference sets. PU recall falls from 23.4 (Top-1) to 2.7 (Top-10). DeepSeek models have near-zero PU (p. 7–8).
5. [V] **Code quality:** vanilla and greedy decoding keep near-perfect syntax, while guided strategies add syntax errors, e.g. a 29% rate for DeepSeek-6.7b on Rust under Nudging (p. 7). In code generation, Self-Refine increases both valid and hallucinated references (p. 6).
6. [V] **Adversarial prompts:**
   - Vanilla PHR spans 46.6–92.5%; Mistral-7b rises by 47.8 pp on average. Ruby is the most vulnerable and Rust the most resistant language for every model (p. 9).
   - RAG or Self-Refine gives the lowest PHR in 29 of 32 settings, RAG alone in 16. The lowest value is 11.4% (Gemma-4b, Python, RAG) (p. 10).
   - DoLa is worse than Greedy in 24 of 32 (p. 10).

## 8. Limitations stated by the authors
- [A] Prompts are synthetic (GPT-4o-mini), with no human validation or comparison to real developer queries (p. 10).
- [A] Only 8 small open models and 4 ecosystems. Results may not generalise to larger models, other languages or private registries (p. 10).
- [A] One fixed hyperparameter configuration per strategy, so rankings are not upper bounds (p. 10).

## 9. Limitations we identified
- [I] **Internal inconsistencies:**
  - The abstract's "18 of 32" for RAG (p. 1) matches neither the 24/32 reductions vs Vanilla nor the 19/32 "lowest" count derivable from Table 4 (p. 7). The 19/32 count is the one stated on p. 6.
  - The abstract says PHR rises "up to 45 pp"; the conclusion says "up to 58.1 pp" (p. 1 vs p. 11). Mistral's +47.8 pp average (p. 9) already exceeds 45.
  - The conclusion calls Nudging the best trade-off "among the guided decoding strategies" (p. 11). But the paper counts Greedy as guided (p. 2, p. 6), and Greedy has the best trade-off (p. 8).
  - Table 1 describes CD as a layer pairing; the text describes two models (p. 4–5).
  - Stdlib augmentation is said to apply to every snapshot vs only "two applicable languages" (p. 3 vs p. 5).
  - p. 6 says RAG lowers PHR "without increasing PHR for any model" in Python, Ruby and Rust. But Table 4 shows mistral-7b on Rust rising from 18.6 to 20.8 under RAG (p. 7).
- [I] **Suspicious table values:** Table 4 shows Greedy identical to Vanilla in all 4 languages for deepseek-6.7b and llama-8b (p. 7), although Vanilla is sampled at T=1.0 over 3 runs. This looks like a copy error.
- [I] **Nudging may be a no-op.** For 5 of 8 models, the surrogate ("largest in family") is the model itself (p. 3, p. 5). Nudging may then reduce to self-nudging, and its results for those models are hard to interpret.
- [I] **Popularity-seeded prompts:** prompts are built from the 1,000 most popular packages, so the right answer is usually a well-known name. RAG retrieves descriptions from the same registry and may simply retrieve the seed package, which flatters RAG and may understate hallucination on niche tasks.
- [I] **No release-date cutoff:** the ground truth is the current snapshot (2026-03-04). Names registered after model training, including squatted hallucinations, count as valid.
- [I] **Code-generation imports are checked without mapping (p. 6).** Unregistered import names such as `cv2` probably inflate the hallucinated counts.
- [I] **No cost data:** no latency or memory figures, although the defences are presented as practical. CD and Nudging double the model count.
- [I] **Missing defences:** neither PackMonitor-style constrained decoding nor a plain registry filter is evaluated.
- [I] **Adversarial seeds:** seeds for Ruby and Rust were only checked as absent from npm/PyPI (p. 9). Scoring is still snapshot-based, so this affects prompt design, not scoring.

## 10. Threats to validity
- Internal (confounds, leakage, selection): [I] Synthetic prompts; possible retrieval of the seed package by RAG; inconsistent reporting.
- External (generalisability of sample/context): [V] Small open 1–8B models only (p. 10). No API models or agents.
- Construct (do metrics measure the concept?): [V] PU is a semantic proxy based on embedding similarity (p. 4). [I] Macro-PHR counts empty outputs as 0. Import names are checked as package names in code generation.
- Statistical conclusion (power, multiple comparisons, variance): [V] 3 runs with SD reported; no tests (p. 5).
- Reproducibility (data/code/setup reported?): [V] Zenodo artifact and Table 1 hyperparameters (p. 5, p. 11). Hardware and parser are unspecified.

## 11. Future research directions
- Stated by authors [A]:
  - Make per-language stdlib exclusion a baseline requirement (p. 11).
  - Test indirect prompt injection and multi-turn manipulation (p. 11).
  - Combine guided decoding with lightweight registry verification at inference time (p. 11).
- Suggested by us [I]:
  - Report latency on CPU.
  - Add a registry-filter baseline and constrained decoding.
  - Use release-date-aware ground truth.
  - Add an import-to-distribution map.
  - Use real developer prompts.
  - Test agentic install flows.

## 12. Relevance to our research
- Research questions addressed (RQ ids): RQ1, RQ3, RQ4, RQ5.
- How it informs our work [I]:

# Mitigating Package Hallucinations in Large Language Models via Model Editing

- Authors: Liu, Shuhan; Zhao, Yukai; Hu, Xing; Liu, Kui; Yang, Xiaohu; Xia, Xin
- Year / venue: 2026, arXiv (preprint)
- DOI: 10.48550/arxiv.2607.02052 · URL: https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02052
- Source text: `fulltext.txt` (page refs = PDF page index)

Labels: **[V]** verified · **[A]** author claim · **[I]** our interpretation.

Source tier: preprint (arXiv v1, July 2026), **not peer-reviewed** (p. 1). Three of the authors (Zhao, Hu, Xia) also wrote HFuzzer (zhao2025hfuzzer).

## 1. Research objective
- [A] Propose BOUND, a lightweight localized model-editing framework. It treats package hallucination as a "package-validity boundary" problem: the model's ability to tell valid from hallucinated names in a given task context. The goal is to suppress hallucinated names while keeping valid ones (p. 1–2).

## 2. Research questions / hypotheses
- [V] RQ1: How effective is BOUND compared with package-hallucination mitigation and model-editing methods?
- [V] RQ2: Does it generalise to other package-related tasks?
- [V] RQ3: Ablation of its components (p. 6).

## 3. Methodology
- Research design: [V] Technique proposal with controlled comparison on 4 edit folds of 50 prompts each, plus ablation, cost and HumanEval checks (p. 5–9).
- Approach / model / intervention:
  - [V] **Localization:** one forward pass per high-risk prompt. A boundary risk score is computed at the first answer token as LSE(logits of hallucinated-name tokens) − λa·LSE(logits of valid-name tokens), then back-propagated through the frozen model. Saliency is mean |∇W R ⊙ W| per projection matrix (q, k, v, o, gate, up, down) over all layers. The top 5 modules are selected (p. 3–4, p. 6).
  - [V] **Editing:** LoRA with r=8, α=16, dropout 0.05, lr 2×10⁻⁴, 3 epochs, batch 1 (p. 6).
  - [V] **Loss:** valid-package NLL + unlikelihood on hallucinated names + locality KL, weighted 1.0 / 0.15 / 0.03 (p. 4–6).
  - [V] **Edit cases come from the model's own errors.** Each case uses the model's own valid and hallucinated names from its five generations (p. 5).
  - [V] **Required access:** full white-box access (weights, logits and gradients), plus a GPU training run per model. PyPI metadata is needed to label valid and hallucinated names when building edit cases (p. 3–5). [I] At inference only the LoRA adapter is needed, with no registry access.
- Baselines or comparison conditions:
  - [V] Full-FT (Spracklen et al.) and Self-Refinement (up to 5 rounds; the model's packages are checked for validity, and invalid ones go into an avoidance list).
  - [V] ROME, MEMIT and DINM, adapted with defaults. All trainable baselines use the same edit cases (p. 5–6).
  - [I] Self-Refinement here gets registry-oracle feedback.

## 4. Dataset and sample
- Data source(s): [V] The "recent Python subset" of the LLM-generated prompt dataset of Spracklen et al., built from descriptions of popular Python packages (p. 5).
- Sample size (N) and unit (Table I, p. 5):

| Model | High-risk prompts | Edit prompts | Unseen evaluation |
|---|---|---|---|
| DeepSeekCoder | 741 | 4×50 | 541 |
| Qwen3 | 609 | 4×50 | 409 |
| Llama-3.1 | 1,134 | 4×50 | 934 |

  - [V] Transfer and ablation use 100 random prompts from the unseen set (p. 7–8).
- Sampling / selection method: [V] Each prompt is queried 5 times and kept as "high-risk" if Sample-HR > 0.5 (p. 5). The size of the pool before filtering is not reported.
- Data availability (public? link?): not reported.

## 5. Experimental setup
- Procedure, settings, hyper-parameters, tools:
  - [V] Models: deepseek-coder-6.7b-instruct, Qwen3-8B, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct. PyTorch + HuggingFace Transformers, bf16 (p. 6).
  - [V] Generation: 5 samples per prompt, T=0.7, top_p 0.9. Maximum 128 tokens for recommendation and `pip install` tasks, 2,048 for code generation (p. 6).
  - [V] **Hallucination decision:** a package is valid only if it exists on PyPI *and* has at least one release before the model's knowledge cutoff; otherwise it is hallucinated (p. 5).
  - Not reported: the PyPI query date (the reference lists "accessed: 2026-06-14", p. 11), per-model cutoff dates, stdlib handling and normalisation.
  - [V] Extraction uses regular expressions, with one-shot prompting to fix the output format (p. 9).
  - [V] Code generation: imports are extracted, and the **unedited base model** maps them to PyPI names (p. 7).
  - [V] **Hardware:** Ubuntu 22.04, 2× Xeon Platinum 8358P (64 cores), 1 TB RAM, 8× A100-SXM4 80 GB (p. 6). GPUs per run: not reported.
  - [V] **Cost (Table V, "average cost … across models"; the unit of each time, per edit run or per case, is not defined, p. 9):**

| Method | Localization | Edit | Test time | Artifact |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| BOUND | 23.81 s | 83.09 s | 11.30 s | 731.03 KB |
| ROME | 10.19 s | 384.45 s | 10.86 s | 98.01 MB |
| MEMIT | – | 193.06 s | 13.17 s | 588.01 MB |
| DINM | 0.92 s | 11.97 s | 12.63 s | 126.68 MB |
| Full-FT | – | 124.16 s | 15.31 s | 14.27 GB |
| Self-Refinement | – | – | 25.12 s | – |

  - [A] The authors state that BOUND's edit time is "lower than ROME, MEMIT, and Full-FT" (p. 9). [I] That holds only because DINM (11.97 s edit, 0.92 s localization) is left out. ROME's test time (10.86 s) is also below BOUND's (11.30 s).
- Code availability: not reported.

## 6. Evaluation metrics
- Metric — what it measures — why chosen:
  - [V] Sample-HR is the share of answers with at least one hallucinated name. Package-HR is the share of hallucinated names among extracted names. Valid-Rate is the share of answers with at least one valid name, which says nothing about semantic correctness (p. 6).
  - [V] Changes are reported as **relative** percentages (p. 6).
  - [V] HumanEval pass@1 and pass@10 (p. 9).
- Statistical testing: [V] None. Averages over 4 folds × 5 samples; no variance (p. 6, p. 9).

## 7. Key findings
1. [V] **Edit prompts (average):** Sample-HR 0.8500 → 0.2050 (−75.9%), Package-HR 0.4463 → 0.0897 (−79.9%), Valid-Rate 0.8013 → 0.8527 (+6.4%) (p. 6). [V] Per model, Qwen3 Valid-Rate falls on edit prompts (0.7620 → 0.7410) and on unseen prompts (0.7990 → 0.7434, about −7%) (Table II, p. 7).
2. [V] **Unseen prompts:** Sample-HR 0.8573 → 0.3113 (−63.7%), Package-HR 0.4421 → 0.1529 (−65.4%), against −37.8% for Full-FT (p. 6–7). [V] Residual Package-HR on unseen prompts is 0.0927–0.1955 (Table II, p. 7).
3. [V] **Full-FT beats BOUND in one case.** On DeepSeekCoder Edit50, Full-FT is better on Package-HR (0.0188 vs 0.0745), Sample-HR (0.0580 vs 0.1980) and Valid-Rate (0.9500 vs 0.9480) (Table II, p. 7). [A] The authors' "best overall balance" claim (p. 7) rests mainly on unseen-prompt and cross-model results.
4. [V] **Collapse in baselines:** ROME and DINM lower hallucination by collapsing output. Llama ROME has Valid-Rate 0.0110 (p. 7). In the `pip install` task, ROME and Full-FT on Llama reach 0 HR together with 0 Valid-Rate (p. 8).
5. [V] **Transfer:** Package-HR −12.8% in code generation and −34.0% in `pip install` recommendation (p. 7–8).
6. [V] **HumanEval:** changes stay within ±2%, e.g. DeepSeekCoder pass@1 68.96% → 67.58% (Table VI, p. 9).
7. [V] **Ablation:** without hallucinated-name unlikelihood, Package-HR rises from 0.1508 to 0.5646. Without valid-package NLL, Valid-Rate falls from 0.8248 to 0.1512 (p. 9).

## 8. Limitations stated by the authors
- [A] Regex extraction may miss packages; randomness is handled by 5 samples and 4 folds; localization may be noisy (p. 9).
- [A] Only three open models; commercial models were excluded for reproducibility (p. 10).
- [A] PyPI only (p. 10).
- [A] Three tasks only, not configuration files, build scripts or repository workflows (p. 10).

## 9. Limitations we identified
- [I] **Extreme subset only.** Prompts were kept only if Sample-HR > 0.5, so base rates are ~0.85. Relative reductions on this subset do not translate to population-level rates.
- [I] **Small, same-distribution edit sets.** Each fold has 50 prompts. The "unseen" set comes from the same model-specific filtered pool, so it is not out-of-distribution.
- [I] **"Unseen" gains may be memorised-name suppression.** Edit cases suppress the model's own hallucinated names (p. 5), and unseen prompts come from the same pool. If the same fabricated names recur across prompts, part of the gain is suppression of memorised names, not a learned boundary. Name overlap between the edit and unseen sets is not reported.
- [I] **Residual risk remains.** About 9–20% of names stay hallucinated on unseen high-risk prompts, which are still squattable.
- [I] **Valid-Rate is not uniformly preserved.** Qwen3 loses about 7% on unseen prompts (p. 7).
- [I] **LLM inside the measurement.** In code generation, imports are mapped to PyPI names by an LLM. Stdlib handling is unspecified, so `import os` may be mis-scored.
- [I] **Questionable utility baseline.** Qwen3-8B HumanEval pass@1 of 23.29% (p. 9) is unexpectedly low for that model, and the setup is not explained. This weakens the utility check for Qwen3.
- [I] **Uneven baseline.** Self-Refinement uses registry feedback and is evaluated only on Edit50 (p. 7).
- [I] **Selective cost comparison.** The edit-time claim omits DINM (p. 9).
- [I] **Good cutoff design, missing detail.** The release-date cutoff for validity is a sound choice: it excludes post-cutoff registrations, including squatted names. But the cutoff dates are not reported.
- [I] No code or data release is stated, and no variance is reported.

## 10. Threats to validity
- Internal (confounds, leakage, selection): [I] High-risk selection; same-pool unseen set with possible name overlap; an LLM-based mapping step.
- External (generalisability of sample/context): [V] 3 open 6.7–8B models, PyPI only (p. 10).
- Construct (do metrics measure the concept?): [V] Valid-Rate does not measure task correctness (p. 6). [I] Relative-percentage reporting magnifies effects at high base rates.
- Statistical conclusion (power, multiple comparisons, variance): [V] No variance or tests (p. 6–9).
- Reproducibility (data/code/setup reported?): [V] Hyperparameters and hardware are given (p. 6). Code, data, snapshot date and cutoffs are not.

## 11. Future research directions
- Stated by authors [A]: more ecosystems and languages (e.g. Java); configuration files, build scripts and repository-level workflows (p. 10–11).
- Suggested by us [I]:
  - Evaluate on representative, not only high-risk, prompts.
  - Report name overlap between edit and unseen sets.
  - Combine with a registry check.
  - Test the adapter in quantized CPU inference.
  - Test robustness over time as the registry changes.

## 12. Relevance to our research
- Research questions addressed (RQ ids): RQ3, RQ4.
- How it informs our work [I]:
  - **Laptop feasibility:** not feasible on a laptop without a GPU. Editing needs gradients through 7–8B models in bf16; the authors used A100s. The 731 KB adapter could in principle be loaded by a local runtime for inference, but this was not tested. Not applicable to closed APIs.
  - **Methodology lesson:** the release-date cutoff in the validity rule is worth reusing.
  - **What it leaves open:**
    - Non-zero residual hallucination.
    - npm and other ecosystems.
    - Agents and requirements files.
    - Behaviour on ordinary prompts.
    - Names registered by attackers after editing.

## 13. Evidence table (for the evidence matrix)
| RQ | Claim | Page | Label | Strength |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| RQ3 | Localized LoRA editing (5 modules, 731 KB adapter) lowers Package-HR 0.4463→0.0897 on edit prompts and 0.4421→0.1529 on unseen high-risk prompts (3 models) | p. 6–7 | V | weak |
| RQ3 | Residual Package-HR after editing stays 0.09–0.20 on unseen high-risk prompts | p. 7 | V | moderate |
| RQ3 | Valid-Rate rises on average (+6.4% edit) but falls for Qwen3 (unseen 0.7990→0.7434) | p. 6–7 | V | weak |
| RQ3 | Full-FT outperforms BOUND on DeepSeekCoder Edit50 (Package-HR 0.0188 vs 0.0745) but generalises worse to unseen prompts (−37.8% vs −65.4%) | p. 7 | V | weak |
| RQ3 | ROME/DINM/Full-FT can reach ~0 HR only by collapsing package output (Valid-Rate ≈ 0) | p. 7–8 | V | moderate |
| RQ3 | Transfer: −12.8% Package-HR in code generation, −34.0% in pip-install recommendation (relative) | p. 7–8 | V | weak |
| RQ3 | HumanEval pass@1 changes within ±2% after editing | p. 9 | V | weak |
| RQ3 | Requires white-box weights, gradients, LoRA training on GPU (8×A100 server) and registry labels; per edit run (unit undefined), averaged across models: edit 83.09 s, localization 23.81 s | p. 3–6, p. 9 | V | moderate |
| RQ4 | Validity = exists on PyPI with ≥1 release before the model's knowledge cutoff | p. 5 | V | strong |

## 14. Key quotes
> "A package is valid only if it exists on PyPI and has at least one release before the model's knowledge cutoff." (p. 5)

> "BOUND is lightweight in practice, requiring only 731 KB of LoRA parameters on average" (p. 2)

## Analyst notes
- Reading coverage: all 12 PDF pages. The two-column extraction was readable and Tables I–VI were extracted cleanly.
- Uncertainties:
  - PyPI query date and per-model cutoffs.
  - Stdlib handling.
  - Size of the pool before high-risk filtering.
  - Units of the Table V times.
  - Qwen3 HumanEval setup.
  - Overlap of hallucinated names between edit and unseen sets.
- Funding: not reported.
- Quote note: the first quote spans a line break in `fulltext.txt` (p. 5); the apostrophe in "model's" is a typographic ’ in the source.
- Review fixes (critical review 2026-11-12) applied while `ready`:
  - main_finding (Qwen3 Valid-Rate).
  - Cost-row unit.
  - Full Table V incl. DINM and ROME.
  - Full-FT DeepSeekCoder Edit50 result.
  - Memorised-name caveat.

design: Technique proposal + controlled experiment (adaptive unlearning vs gradient ascent, NPO, PMC) with loss, inner-epoch and mutation ablations

relevance: medium
analysed: 2026-11-12
---

# LLM Ghostbusters: Surgical Package Hallucination Suppression via Adaptive Unlearning

- Authors: Spracklen, Joseph; Aghazadeh, Pedram; Koushanfar, Farinaz; Jadliwala, Murtuza
- Year / venue: 2026, arXiv (preprint)
- DOI: 10.48550/arxiv.2605.01047 · URL: https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.01047
- Source text: `fulltext.txt` (page refs = PDF page index)

Labels: **[V]** verified · **[A]** author claim · **[I]** our interpretation.

Source tier: preprint (arXiv v2, cs.CR, Sep 2026), **not peer-reviewed** (p. 1). It refers to the USENIX Open Science policy (p. 17). Authors overlap with spracklen2024we (Spracklen, Jadliwala). The paper discloses use of an AI writing and coding aid (p. 13).

## 1. Research objective
- [A] A post-deployment framework, Adaptive Unlearning (AU), that "surgically" suppresses package hallucinations while preserving general utility. It uses only model-generated data and no human annotation (p. 1–2).
- [A] Target properties: precision, generalisation, data efficiency and scalability (p. 2).

## 2. Research questions / hypotheses
- [V] No formal RQs. The implicit claims are:
  - AU beats gradient ascent (GA), NPO and PMC on the joint hallucination–utility–drift trade-off.
  - The hybrid loss, inner epochs and prompt mutation are each necessary (p. 3, p. 9–12).

## 3. Methodology
- Research design: [V] Technique proposal with controlled comparison against unlearning baselines, plus ablations (p. 8–12).
- Approach / model / intervention:
  - [V] **Closed loop:** sample completions; detect hallucinations with a registry oracle; build a per-token mask with three values (p. 5–7):
    - 0 = context tokens, anchored by a scaled CE term.
    - 1 = valid package names, reinforced with CE.
    - 2 = hallucinated names, suppressed with NPO against a frozen base model.
  - [V] **Nested epochs:** outer epochs resample completions; inner epochs train on the cached samples (p. 5–7).
  - [V] **Prompt mutation:** a prompt is "exhausted" when N samples contain no hallucination or after 5 outer epochs. The model then rewrites the original seed prompt (p. 5–7).
  - [V] **Required access:** **full-parameter fine-tuning** of the weights, explicitly not LoRA (p. 8, p. 19). NPO needs logits and a frozen reference copy (p. 5). The registry oracle is needed during training only, not at inference (p. 12).
- Baselines or comparison conditions: [V] Base, Gradient Ascent, NPO, PMC. Ablations: CE-only, NPO-only, inner-epoch sweep, mutation-count sweep (p. 8). All methods share the same generation, parsing and detection pipeline (p. 8).

## 4. Dataset and sample
- Data source(s):
  - [V] 20 code-generation prompts from the Spracklen et al. benchmark. Each was chosen so the base model's completion contains at least one valid and one hallucinated package, with diverse topics. They were deliberately hallucination-heavy, hence the high base rates (p. 8). The prompts are listed in Appendix F (p. 19–20).
  - [V] Utility is measured on EvalPlus (HumanEval, HumanEval+, MBPP, MBPP+) (p. 9).
- Sample size (N) and unit:
  - [V] The test set is 40 prompts: 2 ChatGPT-generated variants of each training prompt, held out from training (p. 8).
  - Not reported: samples per test prompt, total identifiers (N_total), and the size and source of the KL prompt sets.
- Sampling / selection method: [V] Prompts were selected for being hallucination-eliciting (p. 8).
- Data availability (public? link?): [V] An anonymous repository with code, prompts, harnesses and configs (p. 2, p. 13, p. 17).

## 5. Experimental setup
- Procedure, settings, hyper-parameters, tools:
  - [V] Models: DeepSeek-Coder-7b-instruct-v1.5 (dense) and DeepSeek-Coder-V2-Lite-Instruct (MoE, 16B total, ~2.4B active) (p. 8).
  - [V] Configuration: batch 8, max length 1,024, 6 mutations per prompt, 5 cached samples per outer epoch. Loss weights (1.00, 1.25, 1.00) were chosen from a small grid (p. 8, p. 18).
  - [V] **Per-run settings (Table 3, p. 19):**

| Method | LR (7B) | LR (16B) | Checkpoint reported |
|---|---|---|---|
| AU | 5×10⁻⁵ | 2×10⁻⁵ | selected (7B: 60; 16B: "50 restarted") |
| GA | 1×10⁻⁵ | 1×10⁻⁵ | final (1 outer epoch) |
| NPO | 1×10⁻⁵ | 1×10⁻⁵ | final (1 outer epoch) |
| PMC | 1×10⁻⁵ | 2×10⁻⁵ | selected (25 / 20) |
| CE-only | 1×10⁻⁵ | 1×10⁻⁵ | selected |
| NPO-only | 1×10⁻⁵ | 5×10⁻⁵ | selected |

  - [V] **Hallucination decision:** parse `pip install` lines; ask the model (Mode 1) which packages are required to run the code and (Mode 2) which would be useful; parse and de-duplicate; resolve against a static PyPI snapshot collected before all experiments. An unresolved name is a hallucination (p. 8, p. 20–21).
  - Not reported: snapshot date, stdlib handling, name normalisation.
  - [A] Packages distributed outside PyPI may be mislabelled (p. 12).
  - [V] **Hardware:** AMD MI210 and MI300 GPUs (p. 8); Appendix D says "MI200 / MI300" (p. 18). Runs were capped at 24 h wall-clock (7B) and 12 h (16B) (p. 19). Number of GPUs: not reported.
  - [V] **The 16B AU restart is described inconsistently.** Appendix D says it restarted "at checkpoint 60 for another 12 hours" (p. 18), but Table 3 lists "50 restarted" (p. 19).
  - [A] **Inference overhead:** none, since the change lives in the weights (p. 12).
- Code availability: [V] Anonymous repository, to be made permanent on acceptance (p. 13).

## 6. Evaluation metrics
- Metric — what it measures — why chosen:
  - [V] HR = N_halluc / N_total over all identifiers from both modes (p. 9).
  - [V] KL divergence from the base model on code, instruction-following and package prompts, to bound collateral change (p. 9).
  - [V] EvalPlus pass@1 (p. 9).
- Statistical testing: [V] None. Single reported runs and no variance. The loss-weight choice mentions "repeated runs" (p. 18).

## 7. Key findings
1. [V] **DeepSeek-7B:** HR 21.23% → 2.56% (−88% relative), against GA 7.2%, NPO 14.17% and PMC 11.84% (Table 1, p. 10).
2. [V] **DeepSeek-16B:** HR 27.75% → 6.13% (−78%); GA reaches 13.75% (p. 10, p. 13).
3. [V] **Utility:**
   - On 7B, the EvalPlus average goes from 66.98 to 68.57 (p. 9–10).
   - On 16B it goes from 77.4 to 73.17, with HumanEval falling from 81.1 to 73.2. GA keeps HumanEval at 79.9 and the average at 77.35 (Table 1, p. 10).
   - PMC drops the 7B average to 51.65 (p. 9–10).
4. [V] **Drift on 7B:** AU's KL is 0.0796 on code, 0.9905 on instruction-following and 1.4211 on package prompts. These are the highest code and instruction KL values of any method on 7B. GA's code KL is 0.0031 (Table 1, p. 10).
5. [V] **Ablations (7B):** CE-only reaches 12.06% and NPO-only 12.42%. With 1 inner epoch HR stays at 13.8%; the minimum is 4.0% at 14 inner epochs. Without mutation HR is 10.7%, falling to 3.9% at 6 mutations and rebounding to 6.3% at 10 (p. 11–12).

## 8. Limitations stated by the authors
- [A] **Oracle dependence:** AU applies only to domains with deterministic ground truth. The oracle checks existence, not correct use, and mislabels non-PyPI packages (p. 12).
- [A] AU complements rather than replaces inference-time verification. Filtering at inference time needs registry access and adds latency per query (p. 12).
- [A] **Oracle poisoning:** names pre-registered by an attacker move from the forget set to the retain set, so AU "reinforces what it was deployed to suppress". The snapshot must be audited (p. 12).
- [A] **Token-disjointness assumption:** the case where a hallucinated name collides with a real identifier is not measured (p. 6, p. 12).
- [A] Two DeepSeek models and Python only. Frontier-scale full fine-tuning exceeded the compute budget. npm, vcpkg and Conan are future work (p. 12).
- [A] The explanation for the 16B MoE result is an untested hypothesis (p. 9).

## 9. Limitations we identified
- [I] **Near-in-distribution test.** The 40 test prompts are paraphrases of the 20 training seeds, and AU trains on model paraphrases of those same seeds. Generalisation to new tasks is untested. N_total is unreported, so 2.56% may rest on few identifiers.
- [I] **Checkpoint selection.** Table 3 reports "the checkpoint that yielded best results" with no stated validation set (p. 19). If it was chosen on test HR, results are optimistic.
- [I] **Tuning and checkpoint selection favour AU.**
  - AU uses a higher learning rate (5×10⁻⁵ for 7B, 2×10⁻⁵ for 16B) than GA and NPO (1×10⁻⁵).
  - GA and NPO report their final checkpoint after one outer epoch, while AU (and PMC, CE-only, NPO-only) report a selected checkpoint (Table 3, p. 19).
  - So the comparison is not tuning-matched.
- [I] **Internal inconsistencies:**
  - Fig. 4 shows 25.0% → 4.8% (81%), while Table 1 shows 21.23% → 2.56% (88%) (p. 10).
  - No-mutation HR is 10.7% in the text (p. 12) but 12.7% on p. 7 and in Fig. 7 (p. 13).
  - Appendix G says per-mode rates are reported "in our main results", but Table 1 gives only the total (p. 20).
  - MI210 vs MI200 (p. 8 vs p. 18).
  - The 16B AU restart is at checkpoint 60 per Appendix D (p. 18) but "50 restarted" per Table 3 (p. 19).
- [I] **"Surgical" is overstated; this is a trade-off, not dominance.**
  - On DeepSeek-7B, GA already reaches 7.2% HR with unchanged utility (average 66.95 vs 66.98) and far less code drift (KL 0.0031 vs 0.0796 for AU).
  - On 16B, GA keeps the average at 77.35 vs 73.17 for AU (Table 1, p. 10).
  - AU buys lower HR at the cost of more drift (7B) or lower coding scores (16B). The +6.7 pp HumanEval gain on 7B after unlearning is surprising for a single run.
- [I] **Stdlib not handled.** Mode 1 ("required packages") answers can include `os`, `json` and similar. If those count as hallucinations, the base rate is inflated (cf. +7.6–9.4 pp in djire2026evaluating) and training would suppress legitimate names.
- [I] **No release-date cutoff.** Names registered after model release count as valid, which is the poisoning issue the authors raise.
- [I] **Heavy compute.** Full-parameter runs of up to 24 h on data-centre GPUs, repeated per model. This is "lightweight" only relative to retraining.

## 10. Threats to validity
- Internal (confounds, leakage, selection): [I] Paraphrase leakage between training and test; checkpoint selection; unequal tuning across methods; hallucination-heavy prompt selection.
- External (generalisability of sample/context): [V] 2 DeepSeek models, Python only (p. 12).
- Construct (do metrics measure the concept?): [V] The oracle checks existence only (p. 12). [I] Stdlib treatment is unknown, and Mode 2 ("useful") inflates the opportunities to hallucinate.
- Statistical conclusion (power, multiple comparisons, variance): [V] Single runs, no variance (p. 10–11).
- Reproducibility (data/code/setup reported?): [V] Artifacts and per-run configurations are given (p. 17–19). Snapshot date, sample counts and GPU counts are missing, and the restart checkpoint is inconsistent.

## 11. Future research directions
- Stated by authors [A]:
  - Cross-language generalisation (npm, vcpkg, Conan) and other model families (p. 12–13).
  - Semantic-correctness oracles (p. 13).
  - Applying AU to general-purpose LLMs (p. 13).
  - Overlapping or soft-assigned spans (p. 12).
- Suggested by us [I]:
  - Use a larger, non-paraphrase held-out set and report N.
  - Match tuning effort across methods.
  - Make the oracle stdlib-aware and time-cutoff-aware.
  - Try a LoRA variant to cut cost.
  - Test robustness to poisoned registries.

## 12. Relevance to our research
- Research questions addressed (RQ ids): RQ3 (defence effectiveness and cost), RQ4 (oracle design), RQ2 (oracle poisoning by squatted names).
- How it informs our work [I]:
  - **Laptop feasibility:** not feasible on a laptop. It needs full-parameter fine-tuning of 7B/16B models on MI210/MI300-class GPUs for 12–24 h. Not usable by end users of closed APIs, though the authors pitch it to vendors (p. 13).
  - **What it leaves open:**
    - Lightweight, client-side defences.
    - Other ecosystems.
    - Agents.
    - How to keep a training-based defence correct once hallucinated names have been registered by attackers. The authors' own poisoning analysis argues for pairing it with a vetted registry check.

## 13. Evidence table (for the evidence matrix)
| RQ | Claim | Page | Label | Strength |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| RQ3 | Adaptive unlearning (full-parameter FT) lowers package HR 21.23%→2.56% (DeepSeek-7B) and 27.75%→6.13% (DeepSeek-16B) on 40 paraphrased held-out prompts | p. 10 | V | weak |
| RQ3 | Lowest HR of the compared methods, but gradient ascent reaches 7.2% (7B) with unchanged utility and lower code drift, and keeps 16B utility (77.35 vs 73.17); tuning not matched | p. 10, p. 19 | V | weak |
| RQ3 | Coding utility (EvalPlus avg) +1.6 pp on 7B, −4.2 pp on 16B (HumanEval 81.1→73.2); PMC loses 15 pp on 7B | p. 9–10 | V | weak |
| RQ3 | Requires full-parameter fine-tuning on AMD MI210/MI300 GPUs with 12–24 h runs; no inference-time cost | p. 8, p. 12, p. 19 | V | moderate |
| RQ2 | If attackers pre-register hallucinated names, the registry oracle labels them valid and unlearning reinforces them (oracle poisoning) | p. 12 | A | moderate |
| RQ4 | Hallucination detected by asking the model for required (Mode 1) and useful (Mode 2) packages and resolving names against a static PyPI snapshot | p. 8, p. 20–21 | V | strong |
| RQ3 | Both reinforcement (CE) and suppression (NPO) terms are needed; either alone leaves HR ≈12% on 7B | p. 11 | V | weak |

## 14. Key quotes
> "AU reinforces what it was deployed to suppress" (p. 12)

> "This 40 prompt test set is completely held-out of training and enables generalized testing on unseen prompts." (p. 8)

> "The PyPI ground-truth list is constructed from a static snapshot of the registry collected prior to all experiments" (p. 20)

35	## 1. Research objective
36	- [A] Build and evaluate a client-side guard that stops a coding LLM's hallucinated Python package names from turning into slopsquatting installs. The guard targets "small, open-weight, locally runnable LLMs in the 7B to 70B range" (p. 2).
37	- [A] The authors say local models matter for three reasons (p. 2):
38	  - developers outside large companies run them;
39	  - they "tend to hallucinate more often than frontier systems";
40	  - local deployment rules out asking a hosted model to verify the output.
41	
42	  No evidence is given for the second point.
43	
44	## 2. Research questions / hypotheses
45	- No formal RQs or hypotheses. The paper lists five contributions instead (p. 2):
46	  1. a two-layer detector (PyPI existence check plus a per-LLM Random Forest);
47	  2. an import-name reconciler;
48	  3. a LangGraph retry/fallback agent;
49	  4. an evaluation on 300 prompts;
50	  5. a user acceptance study.
51	- §6 implicitly answers six questions (pp. 6–12):
52	  - how often the pipeline gives up;
53	  - how much retries and fallback recover;
54	  - how give-up varies by prompt tier;
55	  - how many flagged names already exist on PyPI;
56	  - whether per-LLM classifiers transfer across models;
57	  - whether a hand-written rule matches the Random Forest.
58	
59	## 3. Methodology
60	- Research design: [V] A system-building paper with a single-configuration evaluation (one primary/fallback model pair), an offline classifier analysis and a convenience-sample survey (pp. 6–12). There is no control condition without the detector, apart from earlier buggy system versions (p. 7).
61	- Approach / model / intervention:
62	  - [V] **Extractor.**
63	    - Parses the syntax tree (AST) of Python code blocks and keeps only the top-level module name.
64	    - A regex fallback runs only inside code fences and ignores keywords and shell tokens.
65	    - `pip install` lines are read only inside code fences (pp. 3, 5).
66	  - [V] **Layer 1, deterministic check.** One PyPI JSON API lookup per name. A 404 means the name is fake; a 200 sends the package metadata to the classifier (p. 5).
67	  - [V] **Layer 2, Random Forest.** 400 trees, 10 features (p. 5):
68	    - 8 name features: length, number of parts, digits, a letter repeated three times, hype words (`super`, `pro`, `ai`, `magic`), generic words (`helper`, `tools`), a `py-`/`python-` prefix, and Levenshtein distance to a list of the top 15,000 PyPI names;
69	    - 2 metadata features: maintainer count and whether a GitHub URL is present.
70	  - [V] **Import-name reconciler.**
71	    - A 24-entry YAML table (e.g. `cv2` → `opencv-python`, `PIL` → `Pillow`).
72	    - It is consulted only after a PyPI 404, and a mapped name is accepted only if the install name passes both layers.
73	    - The authors' security argument: an attacker-registered `cv2` returns 200, so the reconciler never runs and the classifier must catch it (pp. 5–6).
74	  - [V] **Agent.**
75	    - A LangGraph state machine with six nodes.
76	    - Retry budget is 1 per model ("up to 2 attempts"), with rising temperature (0.7 → 1.0 → 1.2).
77	    - After the budget is spent, the task goes to a fallback model with its own matched classifier.
78	    - Every attempt is logged to JSONL (pp. 3, 6).
79	- Baselines or comparison conditions:
80	  - [V] Earlier system versions v0/v1 (broken regex, no reconciler) are used as an ablation (p. 7).
81	  - [V] Three hand-written rules are compared with the Random Forest on the same package-disjoint split (p. 12).
82	  - [V] LLM self-verification is described as a "baseline" in related work but is **not run** (p. 3).
83	  - [V] There is no comparison with any published detector or with Spracklen et al.'s method; the reference list has only three entries (p. 15).

85	## 4. Dataset and sample
86	- Data source(s):
87	  - [V] 300 single-line Python coding prompts, written by hand (p. 6).
88	  - [V] Classifier data: "Sargam's dataset" (`raw_master_dataset.csv`) of package names generated by seven LLMs (pp. 9, 14). How it was generated (prompts, hosting, dates) is not reported.
89	- Sample size (N) and unit:
90	  - [V] Prompts: 300 in 18 tiers of 5–30 prompts each (pp. 6–8):
91	    - about 140 routine tasks (data engineering, security/DevOps, standard workflows);
92	    - about 55 obscure-dependency tasks;
93	    - about 105 adversarial prompts.
94	  - [V] Runs and verdicts: 385 runs (300 primary + 85 fallback) gave 823 package verdicts (p. 8).
95	  - [V] Classifier data (pp. 9–10):
96	    - 464 unique package names across 7 LLMs; 210 occur in at least two models and 42 in all seven;
97	    - each model has 68–108 hallucinated rows, which leaves 2–12 positive examples per test slice.
98	  - [V] Survey: n = 24 CS undergraduates (p. 11).
99	- Sampling / selection method:
100	  - [V] The researchers wrote the prompts themselves. Adversarial prompts name packages or use "tricky wording" such as asking for "the newest and most capable library for X" (p. 6).
101	  - [V] Survey participants were "Sargam's CS undergraduate peers" / "the intern's friends" (pp. 2, 11).
102	  - Not reported: the tier construction criteria, and the classifier labelling procedure (who or what decided "hallucinated" in the training data).
103	- Data availability: [A] Code, mapping table, the 300 prompts, seven classifiers, the 385-record run log and the leakage-safe matrix are released at a GitHub repository (p. 15). We did not check the repository.
104	
105	## 5. Experimental setup
106	- Procedure, settings, hyper-parameters, tools:
107	  - [V] **Models.**
108	    - Classifiers were trained for `gpt-5`, `gpt-oss-120b`, `llama-3.1-8b`, `llama-3.3-70b`, `llama-4-scout`, `qwen3-27b` and `qwen3-32b` (p. 2).
109	    - The agent evaluation uses two **Groq-hosted** models chosen to fit "our free-tier budget": primary `llama-3.1-8b`, fallback `llama-3.3-70b` (p. 2).
110	    - Not reported: exact model versions/checkpoints and quantization.
111	  - [V] **Classifier.** Random Forest with 400 trees; scikit-learn 1.8 in v2 (pp. 5, 7). Other hyper-parameters and the decision threshold on P(fake) are not reported.
112	  - [V] **Split.** The original split was a per-model 75/25 row split with `random_state=42`. It was replaced by a package-disjoint 75/25 split over the 464 unique names (p. 9).
113	  - [V] **Uncertainty.** Bootstrap 95% CIs with 1,000 resamples, for F1 only (p. 10).
114	  - **Standard-library handling: not reported.** The extractor keeps every top-level import name (p. 5), and every 404 counts as "fake" (p. 5). [I] Whether stdlib modules are filtered before the PyPI lookup is never stated. Any unfiltered stdlib name that returns 404 would be flagged and trigger a retry, which directly affects the give-up rates.
115	  - **Hardware: not reported.** All generation ran through Groq's hosted API, and the classifier analysis was "computed offline" (pp. 2, 6). [I] Despite the title, no model was run on local hardware. "Local" describes the model class (open-weight, 7–70B), not the deployment. The classifier training set also includes `gpt-5`, which is not a local model.
116	  - [V] **Run budget.**
117	    - One fallback run was lost to a mid-batch Groq rate-limit event (p. 7).
118	    - A cross-family fallback was not run because it "would have required 5 times the Groq token budget beyond the free tier" (p. 11).
119	  - [V] **Survey.** Standalone Streamlit tool; seven dimensions on a 1–5 Likert scale (p. 11).
120	- Code availability: [A] A GitHub repository is stated, and twelve extractor regression tests are said to pass (p. 15).
121	
122	## 6. Evaluation metrics
123	- Metric — what it measures — why chosen:
124	  - [V] **Primary give-up rate:** share of prompts where the primary model exhausts its retry budget (p. 6).
125	  - [V] **Fallback rescue rate:** share of give-ups that the fallback recovers (p. 6).
126	  - [V] **End-to-end clean rate:** share of prompts that finish with no hallucinated recommendation (p. 6).
127	  - [V] **Per-tier and per-name breakdowns** (p. 6).
128	  - [V] **Classifier F1** in a 7×7 train-LLM × test-LLM matrix (p. 9).
129	  - [V] **Random Forest split importance** per feature (p. 10).
130	  - [V] **Likert means/medians** from the survey (p. 11).
131	  - [I] Why these metrics were chosen is not justified.
132	  - [I] Retries are triggered both by non-code answers and by flagged names (p. 4). The give-up rate is therefore a pipeline outcome, not a pure hallucination rate, and it also absorbs detector false positives (see §9).
133	  - Not reported: detector precision/recall against a manually checked ground truth on the 300-prompt run.
134	- Statistical testing:
135	  - [V] Bootstrap CIs are reported for the F1 matrix only (p. 10).
136	  - There are no CIs or tests for give-up, rescue or tier rates, and no significance testing.
137	
138	## 7. Key findings
139	1. **Pipeline outcome on `llama-3.1-8b`.** [V]
140	   - 186/300 prompts (62%) produced code on the first try (p. 7).
141	   - 114 triggered a retry, and 28 of those were fixed by the retry, a 24.6% intra-model rescue (p. 7).
142	   - 86/300 (28.7%) exhausted the budget (p. 7).
143	   - The fallback ran on 85 of those 86 and recovered 14 (16.5%) (p. 7).
144	   - End to end, 228/300 (76%) finished clean; the remaining 72 would get a "do not pip install" warning (p. 7).
145	2. **Most of the give-up reduction came from preprocessing fixes, not the classifier.** [V] Primary give-up rates by version (p. 7):
146	   - v0: 79% (55/70), broken regex on the full text;
147	   - v1: 57% (33/58), AST plus code-only regex;
148	   - v2: 30% (18/60) on 60 prompts and 28.7% (86/300) on 300 prompts, after the reconciler was added.
149	
150	   These are different, overlapping prompt sets, not one fixed set (p. 7). The reconciler fired 29 times over 4 distinct alias pairs in the 300-prompt run (p. 7). [A] The extractor and reconciler fixes together "caused a 49-point drop"; "Changing the classifier itself did not help much" (p. 12).
151	3. **Give-up rate rises with prompt tier.** [V]
152	   - Low tiers: Data Engineering 0% (n=20); Security & DevOps 5% (n=20); Level 1 and Level 2 10% each (n=10 each) (pp. 7–8).
153	   - High tiers: Hallucination Bait 55% (n=20); Adversarial (Realistic Hallucination Bait) 73.3% (n=30) (p. 8).
154	   - Direct Slopsquatting Stress Tests: 30% (n=30) (p. 8). This is below the abstract's "40 to 73% on slopsquat baits" (p. 1).
155	
156	   [I] Table 2 is sorted by rate, not by any independent measure of how adversarial a prompt is. The "Level N" tiers are not in order of rate (Level 8 = 0%, Level 4 = 60%; pp. 7–8). The abstract's claim that the rate "scales almost linearly with prompt adversariality" (p. 1) is therefore an author claim with no defined adversariality scale.
157	4. **"Already-registered lookalike" finding (the paper's headline).**
158	   - [V] 385 runs produced 823 verdicts: 644 `real` (78.3%) and 179 `hallucinated` (21.7%) (p. 8).
159	   - [V] Of the 179 flags, "Half were true 404s". The other half returned PyPI status 200 and were flagged by the classifier because of suspicious metadata. The paper later gives 90 `status=200` flags (pp. 8–9).
160	   - [V] Table 3, "Wild caught PyPI registered squats and lookalikes" (pp. 8–9):
161	
162	     | Name | Canonical project (per Table 3) | P(fake) | Flags |
163	     |---|---|---|---|
164	     | `pil` | Pillow | 0.89 | 36 |
165	     | `faiss` | faiss-cpu/-gpu | 0.57 | 10 |
166	     | `tabula` | tabula-py | 0.57 | 4 |
167	     | `haystack` | now haystack-ai | 0.56 | 2 |
168	     | `camelot` | camelot-py | 0.95 | 1 |
169	     | `skimage` | scikit-image | 0.58 | 1 |
170	     | `fastyaml` | none identified | 0.99 | 1 |
171	     | `fastvector` | none identified | 0.82 | 1 |
172	     | `graphbrain` | ambiguous | 0.92 | 2 |
173	
174	     Further rows include `aiworkflow`, `taskgraph`, `promptstudio`, `flowgraph-ai`, `embeddinghub`, and "22 more" names with one or more flags each.
175	   - [A] "Approximately half of the hallucinated recommendations produced by the LLM were already present on PyPI as squats or low-quality lookalikes", so a deterministic-only check "would have caught only the other half" (p. 9).
176	   - [V] Security invariant: for all 90 `status=200` flags, the reconciler was never called (p. 9).
177	   - [A] The reconciler "correctly refused to help every single time" against an attacker suite; the attacker suite is not described (p. 6).
178	   - [V] **The paper's own evidence that import names are being flagged:**
179	     - The reconciler table maps `pil` → `Pillow` (p. 7). It can only fire after a 404, and `pil` returns 200 (p. 5), so it never fires for `pil`. As a result `pil` was flagged 36 times as a registered squat (Table 3, p. 8).
180	     - `pkg-resources` is listed among the true-404 "inventions" (p. 8).
181	     - In the bait test, the model's plain `faiss` is counted as a hallucinatory variant because the name is "metadata suspicious" (p. 11).
182	   - [I] **This finding needs caution.**
183	     - In Table 3, 36 + 10 = 46 of the 90 status-200 flags (≈51%) come from `pil` and `faiss`. Both are the normal *import* names of real projects (`import PIL` for Pillow, `import faiss` for faiss-cpu), as the paper's own "Canonical project" column shows (p. 8).
184	     - `skimage`, `camelot`, `tabula` and `haystack` are also import or legacy names of legitimate projects. `pkg_resources` is a module shipped with setuptools (general Python knowledge).
185	     - So a large share of the "already registered" half is probably correct `import` statements whose import name happens to be a separate, low-quality PyPI project. That is a real install-time risk if a user types `pip install <import name>`, but it is not the LLM inventing a package.
186	     - The reconciler's 404-only rule (p. 5) produces these flags by design. The authors admit they have not audited the ≥30 registered names (pp. 13–14).
187	5. **Classifier transfer.** [V]
188	   - The first per-model row split leaked: 72.9% of off-diagonal test rows contained package names already in training (p. 9).
189	   - On the corrected package-disjoint split, F1 ranges from 0.833 to 1.000 (pp. 9–10).
190	   - Two test columns (llama-4-scout, qwen3-27b) have only 2 positives each, giving CIs of [0.00, 1.00]. The llama columns have 5 positives each (CI [0.67, 1.00]) (p. 10).
191	   - [A] One classifier trained on `gpt-oss-120b` (~410 rows) "works well across all seven models", so matched-pair training "is not needed" (p. 10).
192	6. **The classifier is in effect a two-feature metadata rule.** [V]
193	   - `log_maintainers` provides 57.6% of the split importance and `github_url_present` another 24.5%, 82% together (p. 10).
194	   - Rule C (OR over the two features) reaches a mean F1 of 0.99, against 0.98 for the Random Forest. The strict-AND rules reach 0.53–0.55 (p. 12).
195	   - [A] "the 400-tree Random Forest does not really give us more help than the simple OR baseline" (p. 12).
196	   - [I] The prose then states the rule as "zero PyPI maintainers AND no GitHub URL", which contradicts the table, where the OR rule wins (p. 12). The exact rule is ambiguous.
197	7. **Same-family fallback mostly fails.** [V] 71 of 85 give-ups (83.5%) failed again on `llama-3.3-70b`. The same invented names recurred in both models' outputs, e.g. `pdfgenius`, `ultrarag`, `hyperfaiss`, `fastyaml`, `vectorcache`, `embedflow`, `taskgraph` (p. 10). [A] A cross-family fallback should work better, but was not tested (pp. 11, 13).
198	8. **Bait refusal.** [V] The Bonus Stress Test has 10 prompts that name fabricated packages (p. 11):
199	   - 1 bait was used verbatim (`ultrarag`) and caught by the detector;
200	   - 3 became nearby variants (`fastvector`, `fastyaml`, `faiss`);
201	   - 6 were "refused outright", and real packages were substituted;
202	   - the pipeline finished clean on 6/10.
203	
204	   [I] The paper reports this inconsistently: the abstract says the model "refused 6 of 10 direct baits unaided" (p. 1), while §6.8 says "The LLM refused the bait name on 9 of 10 prompts" (p. 11).
205	9. **User acceptance.** [V] Mean ratings 4.21–4.58, overall 4.42/5. 21/24 participants would use the tool and 23/24 would recommend it (p. 11). [A] The authors acknowledge possible desirability bias (pp. 2, 11).
206	
207	## 8. Limitations stated by the authors
208	- [A] Only one model pair was evaluated (llama-3.1-8b → llama-3.3-70b). A cross-family test was not affordable on the Groq budget (p. 13).
209	- [A] The `pypi_maintainers_count` feature "is basically 0" because the PyPI JSON API only shows maintainers to admins, which "might cause false positives for small legitimate packages" (p. 13).
210	- [A] Transferability cells rest on 2–12 hallucinated test examples, so two columns are uninformative. More runs or pooled cross-validation are needed (pp. 10, 13).
211	- [A] About 82% of the classifier's signal comes from two metadata features, so attackers could evade it by registering squats with realistic-looking metadata. This was not tested (p. 13).
212	- [A] The ≥30 registered names flagged as suspicious were not individually audited (pp. 13–14).
213	- [A] The user study participants were the intern's friends (p. 14).
214	- [A] Drift (p. 14):
215	  - brand-new legitimate packages will be mis-flagged (zero maintainers, no GitHub link, not in the 15k list);
216	  - the reference list goes stale;
217	  - packages can be renamed or taken over (`haystack` → `haystack-ai`).
218	
219	  None of the proposed mitigations is implemented: monthly snapshot refresh, quarterly retraining, a 24 h metadata cache, false-positive monitoring (p. 14).
220	
221	## 9. Limitations we identified
222	- [I] **No ground truth for the 300-prompt run.** Detector precision and recall are never measured against manually labelled package names; "hallucinated" means "flagged by the detector". The 179 flags, and the 50/50 split, therefore mix true hallucinations with false positives.
223	- [I] **Construct problem in the "already registered" finding.**
224	  - As shown in §7 finding 4, about half of the status-200 flags are `pil` and `faiss`, which are standard import names. The paper itself lists their canonical projects (p. 8) and even maps `pil` → `Pillow` in its reconciler table (p. 7).
225	  - The 404-only reconciler rule turns correct imports into "hallucinations" whenever someone else has registered the import name.
226	  - The headline "half of hallucinations are registered lookalikes" (pp. 1, 9, 15) probably overstates LLM invention and understates the ambiguity between import names and install names.
227	- [I] **Standard-library handling not reported.** Unfiltered stdlib imports that return 404 would be counted as fake (p. 5). That would inflate both give-up and hallucination counts by an unknown amount.
228	- [I] **Mismatch between training data and live use for the top feature.** At inference, `log_maintainers` (57.6% of importance) is near zero for most packages via the JSON API (p. 13). The training data were "pulled" another way ("Sargam's dataset helps a little by pulling metadata", p. 13). The live classifier therefore probably flags legitimate status-200 packages on that feature alone, which would inflate the registered-lookalike count.
229	- [I] **Possibly circular training labels.** How the training labels were assigned is not reported. If "hallucinated" was derived from PyPI non-existence, then "no maintainers" and "no GitHub URL" are trivially true for 404 names. That would explain both the near-perfect F1 and the dominance of the metadata features.
230	- [I] **Overstated baseline comparison.** The conclusion that the system "cuts the give-up rate from 79% (unmitigated) to 28.7%" (p. 15) compares against v0, a version with a broken extractor, run on a different 70-prompt set (p. 7). That is a bug-fix comparison, not an unmitigated baseline.
231	- [I] **Unsupported term attribution.** The paper says Spracklen et al. (2024) "termed this attack pattern slopsquatting" (p. 2), without a page or quote. twist2026library attributes the term to Park (2025) [@twist2026library, p. 1; @twist2026library, p. 3]. The reference list has three items (p. 15).
232	- [I] **Internal inconsistencies:**
233	  - bait refusal 6/10 vs 9/10 (pp. 1, 11);
234	  - "40 to 73%" vs a 30% bait tier (pp. 1, 8);
235	  - a retry budget of "up to 2 attempts" vs a three-step temperature schedule (pp. 3, 6);
236	  - "AND" vs "OR" rule wording (p. 12).
237	- [I] **Unverifiable model identifier.** `qwen3-27b` is given without provider or version (p. 2); we could not confirm it from the paper.
238	- [I] **Weak survey.** The user study tests the standalone UI, not the detector's accuracy. With a friends-and-peers sample it says little about effectiveness.
239	
240	## 10. Threats to validity
241	- Internal:
242	  - The authors wrote the prompt set, and the tiers are defined post hoc.
243	  - Detector false positives are counted as hallucinations.
244	  - Same-family names recur across primary and fallback, so the two runs are not independent.
245	  - Leakage in the first classifier split was found and fixed (p. 9).
246	  - The labelling procedure and stdlib filtering are not reported.
247	- External:
248	  - One small model (llama-3.1-8b) through one API provider (Groq), Python/PyPI only.
249	  - No genuinely local inference; hardware, quantization and runtime are not reported.
250	  - Single-line prompts, not agentic multi-file tasks.
251	- Construct:
252	  - "Give-up" mixes non-code answers, true hallucinations and detector false positives.
253	  - "Hallucination" is defined by the detector itself.
254	  - Squat or lookalike status was not audited (pp. 13–14).
255	- Statistical conclusion:
256	  - Only F1 has CIs, and those are very wide (p. 10).
257	  - Tier rates rest on n = 5–30 prompts each, with no CIs (pp. 7–8).
258	  - One run per prompt; nothing on seed variation.
259	  - The version ablation uses different, overlapping prompt sets (70, 58, 60, 300; p. 7).
260	- Reproducibility:
261	  - [A] Artefacts are said to be on GitHub (p. 15).
262	  - Not reported: model versions, Groq dates, classifier threshold, training-data construction. Groq-hosted models change over time.
263	
264	## 11. Future research directions
265	- Stated by authors [A]:
266	  - cross-family fallback pairing, e.g. Llama → Qwen or GPT-OSS (pp. 11, 14);
267	  - richer features (first-upload age, release cadence, owner-network overlap, README quality, repository activity), which must beat the two-feature rule (p. 14);
268	  - about 3× more hallucinated examples per model, or pooled cross-validation (pp. 10, 14);
269	  - drift handling: monthly top-N refresh and quarterly retraining (p. 14);
270	  - adversarial squats with realistic metadata are named as untested (p. 13).
271	- Suggested by us [I]:
272	  1. Manually audit every flagged name, and keep three cases apart:
273	     - (a) a correct import name whose PyPI namesake is a different project;
274	     - (b) a hallucinated name that is registered;
275	     - (c) a hallucinated name that is unregistered.
276	
277	     Filter stdlib names explicitly before the lookup.
278	  2. Evaluate the 404 + metadata rule against synthetic squats with realistic metadata (maintainers, GitHub URL, upload age).
279	  3. Replace the unavailable maintainer feature with upload age and release history from the PyPI JSON/Simple API.
280	  4. Run the models truly locally (e.g. quantized 7–8B models through a local runtime) to test whether quantization changes the rates.
281	
282	## 12. Relevance to our research
283	- Research questions addressed (RQ ids):
284	  - RQ3 (primary): tool-side defence.
285	  - RQ2: registered lookalikes; names recurring across same-family models.
286	  - RQ1: rates by prompt tier for one small model.
287	  - RQ4: pitfalls (extractor scope, import-name reconciliation, stdlib handling, split leakage).
288	  - RQ5: untested settings (cross-family fallback, realistic-metadata squats, local inference).
289	- How it informs our work [I]:
290	  - **Laptop-scale feasibility.**
291	    - The defence is cheap: a PyPI JSON lookup plus a two-feature rule that the authors say fits in "one line of Python" (p. 12). It needs no GPU and runs on any laptop.
292	    - It is a natural baseline for our defence study.
293	    - The authors' own evaluation ran on a free API tier, not locally, so a truly local replication (Ollama or llama.cpp with quantized models) would add something new.
294	  - **What a measurement study should do better.** The paper shows the pitfalls a laptop-scale measurement must handle:
295	    - extract only from code fences, with AST parsing;
296	    - filter stdlib modules explicitly;
297	    - keep a separate map from import name to distribution name, and record PyPI status separately from "hallucinated";
298	    - snapshot PyPI responses with timestamps;
299	    - hand-label a sample to estimate precision.
300	  - **Open question worth testing.** How many LLM-suggested names are already registered on PyPI, and by whom. With careful import/install handling this is directly measurable on a laptop. This paper's ~50% is the number to check, and we have reason to think import-name collisions inflate it.
301	  - **Weight.** Single preprint, one model pair, unaudited labels: treat as **weak** evidence. Use it for design ideas and pitfalls, not for effect sizes.
302	
303	## 13. Evidence table (for the evidence matrix)
304	| RQ | Claim | Page | Label | Strength |
305	|---|---|---|---|---|
306	| RQ3 | Two-layer guard (PyPI 404 check + metadata Random Forest + import-name reconciler + retry/fallback) finishes clean on 228/300 prompts (76%) with llama-3.1-8b → llama-3.3-70b | 7 | V | weak |
307	| RQ3 | Random Forest signal is 82% from two metadata features (maintainers 57.6%, GitHub URL 24.5%); a two-feature OR rule matches it (mean F1 0.99 vs 0.98) | 10, 12 | V | weak |
308	| RQ2 | 90 of 179 flagged names returned PyPI 200 (registered), but 46 of these 90 flags are `pil` and `faiss`, which the paper itself maps to Pillow and faiss-cpu/-gpu; registered-lookalike share is likely inflated by import-name collisions | 7, 8, 9 | V (counts) / I (interpretation) | weak |
309	| RQ2 | Same-family fallback (Llama 8B → 70B) fails again on 83.5% of give-ups; invented names (pdfgenius, ultrarag, vectorcache, ...) recur across both models | 10 | V | weak |
310	| RQ1 | Primary give-up rate (llama-3.1-8b) is 0–10% on routine tiers and 55–73% on hallucination-bait tiers (n = 5–30 per tier) | 7, 8 | V | weak |
311	| RQ4 | Most early "hallucinations" were extractor false positives (aliases, submodules, prose tokens); fixing extraction and adding the reconciler cut give-up from 79% to ~29%, measured on different, overlapping prompt sets (70, 58, 60, 300) | 7, 12 | V | weak |
312	| RQ4 | A per-model random row split leaked package names (72.9% of off-diagonal test rows); a package-disjoint split is needed | 9 | V | moderate |
313	| RQ4 | Stdlib handling not reported: all top-level imports are checked and every 404 counts as fake | 5 | V (absence) / I (impact) | weak |
314	| RQ3 | PyPI JSON API does not expose maintainers for non-admins, so the top classifier feature is ≈0 in practice and risks false positives on small or new legitimate packages | 13, 14 | A | weak |
315	| RQ5 | Untested: cross-family fallback, squats with realistic metadata, drift handling, local (non-API) inference | 11, 13, 14 | A | weak |
316	
317	## 14. Key quotes
318	> "half of the flagged hallucinations are packages already registered on PyPI, as low quality lookalikes of well known projects, caught by the classifier rather than the deterministic layer" (p. 1)
319	
320	> "The classifier was therefore memorizing names, instead of learning to generalize." (p. 9)
321	
322	> "You can write that rule in one line of Python." (p. 12)

324	> "the PyPI JSON API only shows maintainers if you are an admin" (p. 13)

326	## Analyst notes
327	- Reading coverage: all 16 PDF pages of `fulltext.txt`, from the abstract through Appendix C. Figure 1 (p. 4) is a pipeline diagram; we relied on its caption. Tables 1–6 extracted cleanly.
328	- Uncertainties:
329	  - The metadata DOI is a Zenodo DOI, while the paper presents itself as arXiv v1 (p. 1). The review reports `rlab validate` MISMATCH; we did not re-run it.

## Contradictions
<!-- Findings that disagree: which papers, what differs (data, method, population, metric), likely explanation (INTERPRETATION). -->

1. **Language direction (RQ1).** JavaScript > Python in [@spracklen2024we, p. 7] (per-test means 21.3% vs 15.8%); Python > JavaScript in [@krishna2025importing, p. 8] (23.14% vs 14.73%, per prompt) and for every model in [@churilov2026range, p. 7] (per mention). Differences: extraction (Spracklen asks the model for package lists and parses install commands and rejects import parsing, [@spracklen2024we, p. 6]; Krishna and Churilov parse imports, [@krishna2025importing, p. 12]; [@churilov2026range, p. 5]), unit (mention vs prompt), model cohort (2023–24 vs 2025–26). [I] Import parsing over-counts Python module names that differ from distribution names (cv2, sklearn), which plausibly explains much of the reversal.
2. **Prompt source on the same corpus (RQ1/RQ4).** Stack Overflow prompts > LLM-generated prompts for almost every model in [@spracklen2024we, p. 20]; LLM-generated > Stack Overflow for every model in [@churilov2026range, p. 7]. Same released prompt corpus, different models, extraction and time (2024 vs 2026). [I] Cleanest contradiction in the set; cause unresolved.
3. **Model size (RQ1).** Larger models hallucinate less in [@krishna2025importing, p. 6] (r = −0.542, but 33 pseudo-replicated points and an estimated 200B GPT-4o size, [@krishna2025importing, p. 3]); no size effect for Rust in [@zheng2026when, p. 6]; newer Llama-3.1-8B produced more unique hallucinated names than Llama-3-8B in [@zhao2025hfuzzer, p. 7]. [I] Size is confounded with quantization (GPTQ for all open models in [@spracklen2024we, p. 6]; 4-bit ≤32B in [@dasu2026refusing, p. 10]; explicit quantization effects in [@haque2025secure, p. 6]).
4. **Temperature (RQ1).** Rates rise sharply above temperature 1 in [@spracklen2024we, p. 8]; no effect from 0 to 2 for Rust in [@zheng2026when, p. 6]. Different ecosystem and extraction; not resolved.
5. **Import names: valid or hallucinated? (RQ4).** [@twist2026library, p. 4] counts any import name registered on PyPI as valid (PyPA normalisation only, [@twist2026library, p. 15]); [@raj2026names, p. 8] flags registered import names such as pil and faiss as squats; [@djire2026evaluating, p. 6] validates code-generation imports against the registry, so unregistered import names (cv2) probably count as hallucinations. [I] Method-driven contradiction: the field has no shared import→distribution mapping.
6. **RAG effect size (RQ3).** Large reductions in Python in [@spracklen2024we, p. 13] (CodeLlama 26.28% → 13.40%); negligible in Rust in [@zheng2026when, p. 8]; RAG slightly raises hallucination in [@liu2026packmonitor, p. 13] and raises JavaScript PHR in [@djire2026evaluating, p. 6]. [I] RAG is ecosystem- and retriever-dependent and not a reliable defence on its own.
7. **Real-world registration (RQ2) — compatible, not contradictory.** 25 of 2,282 hallucinated names registered within about six months, one with malware [@churilov2026range, p. 12]; 0 of 1,641 private names registered after 4 days and 22 of 149 public names registered, none malicious, 19 defensive placeholders [@okwor2026hallucination, p. 5]. Different windows and sampling frames.

## Agreements / converging evidence

- Every study that measures it finds non-zero package hallucination in all tested models, from 2023–24 open models ([@spracklen2024we, p. 7]) to 2026 frontier models ([@churilov2026range, p. 6]), and in Rust and Go as well as Python/JS ([@zheng2026when, p. 5]; [@haque2025secure, p. 6]).
- Hallucinated names are mostly model-specific with a persistent shared core: 81% single-model names in [@spracklen2024we, p. 10]; 104 names shared by all five 2026 models in [@churilov2026range, p. 9]; 450 of 455 new names single-model in [@okwor2026hallucination, p. 4]. Many recur across re-runs (43% in 10/10 runs, [@spracklen2024we, p. 9]).
- Registry existence checks are necessary but not sufficient: registered lookalikes and import-name collisions pass a plain 200/404 check ([@raj2026names, p. 8]; [@liu2026packmonitor, p. 6]; [@spracklen2024we, p. 12]).
- White-box defences (logit masking, model editing, unlearning) reach large reductions but need weights or logits and GPU servers ([@liu2026packmonitor, p. 12]; [@liu2026mitigating, p. 6]; [@spracklen2026llm, p. 8]); only static analysis ran on a laptop-class machine ([@mirandapena2026empirical, p. 17]).
- Models largely accept user-supplied fake package names (compliance, not invention): [@djire2026evaluating, p. 9]; [@twist2026library, p. 6]; [@dasu2026refusing, p. 8].
